title: How the Early Dreams of the Internet Changed
excerpt: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
body: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
During the 1984 Super Bowl, an advertisement launched a technological revolution
If you were alive, you probably know the one
Directed by Ridley Scott, the minute-long spot showed men in gray uniforms, heads shaved, eyes blank, marching in unison toward a lifeless auditorium

A Big Brother figure speaks from a giant screen, droning on about “the first glorious anniversary of the Information Purification Directives.” All the while, a woman in red shorts and a white tank top is running to the auditorium
She looks like she’s just come from an aerobics class, but she has a sledgehammer, and authorities are in pursuit
Entering the room, she hurls the sledgehammer into Big Brother’s face
There’s a flash of light, and a wind blows over the stunned, awakened audience
A different voice—a comforting one—announces, “On January 24th, Apple Computer will introduce Macintosh
And you’ll see why 1984 won’t be like 1984 .” Although the ad did not show an actual Macintosh computer, it worked
Apple went on to sell 250,000 of its user-friendly, mouse-driven little machines in that year alone
The ad also asserted what was to be a defining idea of the emerging digital age: that personal computers, far from massive instruments of centralized control, were vessels of individual freedom

The coming of the internet, with its invitation to universally accessible knowledge and the free exchange of ideas, seemed to affirm the promise: Our machines wouldn’t enslave us; they would liberate us
The dystopia depicted in the ad came by way of George Orwell’s imagination, but the fears underlying it had deep American roots
As mass consumer culture expanded in the early 20th century, American artists, intellectuals, and critics worried over the problem of “conformity” and the loss of individualism that came with it
Most didn’t see the dark totalitarianism of 1984 ; instead, they saw a world of ready-made desires, a soulless existence brought to you by corporations, advertisers, media, and politicians

As The Atlantic ’s review of Sinclair Lewis’s Babbitt put it in 1922, “the ‘standardized American’” was becoming “as much a national product as the Ford car”—a person like Babbitt himself, whose entire life and very personality were shaped by forces beyond him
Such criticism formed a fault line that ran from the cultural commentary of the ’20s to the outbursts of Beats , folkies, and academics in the ’50s
The earthquake, of course, would come in the counterculture of the 1960s
No longer would people need to be stuffed into “ Little Boxes ,” as the folk singer Malvina Reynolds worried early in the decade
The counterculture promised liberation from such confinement

Visiting San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury district for The Atlantic in 1967, the novelist Mark Harris wondered whether he was seeing Babbitt’s descendants finally rebelling against conformity in ways that Babbitt himself could not

The counterculture’s sensibilities migrated into the mainstream, where popular culture and advertising absorbed its language of liberation and transgression, so that admen could pitch 7 Up using hippie iconography or Virginia Slims cigarettes by way of the women’s-liberation movement
Digital culture would prove especially receptive to these countercultural ideals
Northern California, after all, was the center of both the counterculture and the tech industry, and the cross-pollination between the two was considerable, as the historian Fred Turner has shown
By the 1990s, as the internet was becoming a mass medium, some of its first boosters (many of whom had roots in the counterculture) were presenting it as the realization of countercultural ideals
John Perry Barlow, a poet and sometimes Grateful Dead lyricist, wrote his 1996 “Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace” in response to an early effort to regulate the internet
It reads like a Port Huron Statement for digital culture, describing a realm of individual freedom and free-flowing ideas that would break from existing forms of cultural and institutional authority
According to Barlow, a new “civilization of the Mind” was coming
In the dot-com and digital revolutions that followed, many of the people who sold the hardware, coded the software, and built the platforms were seen as iconoclasts themselves
Digital entrepreneurship became a form of transgression, not just in the casual dress and informal culture of the Silicon Valley office but also in what it promised to users
Tech visionaries pledged to create a world that would make possible precisely the kind of self-expression, open exchange, and communal connection that the counterculture had promised

It was no coincidence that by the late 1990s, Apple’s advertising—again with almost no reference to the machines themselves—simply pictured groundbreaking figures such as Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., Bob Dylan, and John Lennon, alongside the slogan “ Think Different .” In many ways, those promises were fulfilled
The internet did splinter 20th-century mass culture, and the effects have been every bit as revolutionary as promised

We don’t all watch the same networks anymore; we don’t see the same movies; we don’t get our news from the same places or read the same books ( mostly, we just don’t read ); we “ do our own research .” Even as the conditions of mass culture and conformity that shaped the counterculture and the early dreams of the internet have faded, we continue to live in their shadow

In the fractured age of social media and the unknowable algorithm, our devices give us the feeling of freedom, even as they serve the interests of corporate forces that track our movements, catalog our interests, and profile our wants
The oppressive monoculture has been replaced by countless minicultures, each with their own devoted acolytes; we still inhabit little boxes, partially of our own making
The transgressive ethos, meanwhile, continues to thrive

Subversion is perhaps the dominant language of digital culture, spoken across the political spectrum by podcasters “just asking questions,” wellness gurus swilling at-home health hacks, manosphere kingpins lashing out against wokeness, and lefty influencers denouncing the billionaire class
Everyone, it seems, is hurling a sledgehammer at something.

title: The Hasan Piker Question
excerpt: L ike late-summer humidity, Hasan Piker hangs heavy over the discourse
body: L ike late-summer humidity, Hasan Piker hangs heavy over the discourse
At a rally on Monday, Vice President Vance brought up the hard-left streamer in an attempt to paint the Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as anti-American

Last week, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called Piker’s recent statements about Jewish Americans “dangerous and anti-Semitic.” Senators Jon Ossoff, Cory Booker, and Jacky Rosen said much the same
Facing questions about a totally different set of Piker comments, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez hustled into an elevator
Some Democrats are trying to dismiss the 35-year-old political commentator as irrelevant
He’s just “a streamer in California,” El-Sayed said on Saturday, waving off questions from reporters
Piker himself has spent the past week casting himself as the victim of hysteria. “I have become this media cycle’s ‘trans athletes’ or ‘migrant caravan,’” he posted on X

But it was El-Sayed who first made Piker central to his campaign by bringing him out on the trail, partying poolside with him at an influencer event, and celebrating with him during his Election Night rally

In his thousands of hours of streaming, Piker has produced a dense catalog of comments spanning the spectrum from stupid to incredibly offensive, including several iterations of the phrase “I hate America” and, perhaps most memorably, that “America deserved 9/11.” (He quickly attempted to walk it back .) Piker also flaunts his authoritarian sympathies, calling Mao Zedong “one of the great leaders of this world” and counting the collapse of the Soviet Union among the “catastrophes” of the 20th century

Last week, he warned that “eventually someone is going to come around and take action” against American Jews who are “singularly invested in Israel.” [ Read: What El-Sayed does next matters ] Hasan Piker is part of the conversation now
He has become central to the Republican strategy in Michigan, where El-Sayed will continue to be asked about him
So, too, will Democrats across the country
The question ahead of November is whether their answers will satisfy voters
E l-Sayed has moved away from Piker since winning the primary last month
The streamer has not been on the trail in Michigan. “I have spoken with the good doctor,” Representative Jim Clyburn told reporters of El-Sayed, who has a medical degree. “He has apologized

He says he will not campaign with Piker anymore.” After Piker’s comments last week about American Jews, El-Sayed said in a statement that anti-Semitism is a “scourge” and that “I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk.” When asked about Piker at a meeting with a group of Jewish Democrats on Saturday, though, El-Sayed declined to disavow him. “If you want to make this race about a streamer in California, I just think you’re missing the boat.” Anyone could have predicted the Piker blowback

In March, one of El-Sayed’s primary opponents, Mallory McMorrow, compared Piker to the white-supremacist influencer Nick Fuentes, and leaders of the centrist think tank Third Way wrote a column urging Democrats not to associate with Piker. “Everyone saw it coming from a mile away, so they should’ve been better prepared to handle it,” one Democratic strategist told me

Even some of El-Sayed’s own backers felt similarly. “Not all socialism is toxic to the Democratic brand, but Piker certainly is,” one progressive strategist told me. (None of the Democrat-aligned operatives I reached out to would agree to speak on the record for this story, citing their support for El-Sayed as well as their fear of reprisal from Piker’s rabid online fans.) The Piker drama is a ribbon-wrapped gift to Republicans in a year when so much else—inflation, high gas prices, an unpopular president—is working against them

Mike Rogers, El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, refers to Piker as El-Sayed’s “running mate.” “When I see Abdul El-Sayed campaign around this state with somebody who said that America deserved 9/11, what I see is a man who has sympathy and compassion for people who share his religion, but has nothing for people who don’t,” Vance said at the rally on Monday. “What I’d ask you to remember is that whoever you send to Washington, whatever policy views you have or you don’t have, send people of good heart who focus on the right issues, who fight for the right people, and who love the United States of America.” The strategy is obvious: Identify every repellent thing Piker has ever said, tie Piker to El-Sayed, and advertise the relationship at every opportunity
There is more than a hint of irony in this situation
President Trump has shown a strong affinity for shock jocks and trolls
In 2020, he awarded Rush Limbaugh, who had a recurring segment celebrating the deaths of gay people from AIDS, the Presidential Medal of Freedom

Laura Loomer, a far-right activist and an ally of Trump’s, last week referred to a Senate candidate as a “ghetto black communist bitch.” Some Democrats, seeing Trump suffer little political consequence for such associations, believe it’s unfair that El-Sayed should have to answer for Piker’s actions. [ Read: Laura Loomer is a warning ] But politics, like life, is famously unfair
Democrats are constantly being asked to condemn Piker in cable-news hits and hallway interviews, even outside Michigan
Several Jewish Democrats have weighed in too

Through a spokesperson, Ossoff said he “unreservedly rejects reckless and dangerous rhetoric suggesting that policy advocacy invites violence against the Jewish community or any community.” Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey said that “anyone who campaigns with Piker or elevates him is complicit in the rising antisemitism and anti-American hatred in this country.” Moderate Democrats are seizing the moment as a chance to engage in a little centrist posturing
Senator John Fetterman went on Fox News and delivered a challenge to El-Sayed: “I’m offering $50,000 for you to do a rally with Hasan Piker” on September 11, he said
Piker was not immediately available for comment for this story

But last week, after several Jewish Democrats criticized him, he dismissed their concerns by implying they reflected an orchestrated conspiracy against him, writing on X that an “aipac boss call was made.” Maybe El-Sayed could quell some of the frenzy himself
In 2008, controversial comments from Barack Obama’s former pastor Jeremiah Wright threatened to upend Obama’s bid for the White House
In a sermon shortly after September 11, the pastor said that “America’s chickens are coming home to roost.” Later, Wright said, “No, no, no, not God Bless America

God damn America—that’s in the Bible—for killing innocent people.” Obama chose to address the controversy directly, and delivered a speech condemning Wright’s remarks while offering context about America’s racial tensions
That speech “was a masterpiece of empathy, and at the time it felt that it changed the trajectory of his campaign,” Michelle Goldberg wrote this week
At the very least, some Democrats argue, El-Sayed could more plainly denounce his friend. “Say, ‘Here’s what I condemn; here’s what I disavow

I disagree; it was wrong and hurtful,’” the progressive strategist said. “If Piker says something new that’s bad—which, if I was a betting man, I’d say will happen—you come out against it swiftly.” Michigan, a state that Trump won in 2016 and 2024, was never going to be an easy win for El-Sayed
His relationship with Piker, who is paid to provoke, not persuade, isn’t going to make that task any simpler
The good news for Democrats is that most people don’t actually know Piker; polling from earlier this year showed that 60 percent of likely voters have never heard of him
The bad news for Democrats is that Republicans will spend the next two months working diligently to change that.

title: An Alien Scholar’s Notes on Trump’s Washington
excerpt: We’ll start this conference looking back on 2026 Washington Architecture by being honest: We have no idea what happened here
body: We’ll start this conference looking back on 2026 Washington Architecture by being honest: We have no idea what happened here
The snapshot of this planet that my comrades and I managed to obtain on our brief visit left us, if anything, more confused about Earth than we had been before
All we know of 21st-century human political figure Donald J

Trump is what we can guess from the architectural record and a few bits of digital evidence. (Due to a misunderstanding, we ate most of the written records of this planet before figuring out that they contained information.) Was he a builder or a destroyer? There are also ruins of an arch—commemorating a triumph, but over what? Perhaps the successful defeat of 250 years of democracy, a system of rule that he despised? Did he have access to the internet (a human technology that seems to have been primarily used for the sharing of pornography and misinformation)? Impossible to say
Some records suggest that a female of his species accessed the internet on his behalf
We don’t know his exact relation to this female, but we can observe that she was swift of foot and skilled at concealment in small enclosures , probably a trait admired by others

Were such relationships common? Did many human leaders consider it an honor to be chased by another human carrying a printer? (Did George Washington have a “Human Printer” of his own? Perhaps Benjamin Franklin fulfilled this role?) Although other human figures enjoyed construction, Trump seemed to prefer the wrecking ball (what we would refer to as Grogon’s Tail) as a mode of expression
From a forensic analysis of these structures, we know that the Smashing of the Residence was first to take place, followed by the Desecration of the Pool
Donald Trump seems to have smashed the Residence deliberately, as a warning to rivals
As his nestlings were at that time all mature and dwelling independently, such a gesture posed no danger to his young
Some papers we found suggested that there were plans to put something in the enormous hole, but these drawings are on an unlikely scale, and their suggested purpose is inconsistent
Ballroom? Bunker? No one can seem to agree, not even the plans themselves

We may never know why Donald Trump hated the pool (pond?) so much, but his action to strip it of its water, paint over its interior with a humiliating sealant, and fill it with a thick green algae speaks of immense disrespect

Had the pool or pond offended him? We know from the many banners he left bearing his visage around the city that he seems to have been incapable of smiling; a golden idol located in Florida represents him as having a slightly melted appearance

Perhaps glimpsing his reflection in the pond reminded him unpleasantly of these facts? Or were its ducks hostile to him? Some records show that even when the pool was drained of water, it was patrolled by an armed guard; what danger lurked in its shallows? The structure with the giant head in it puzzles us most
We think this site on the Potomac may once have been used for entertainment and functioned as a kind of temple to the performing arts
Others suggest that it was an oversize dwelling place for mice
Some scholars believe that people really went inside the building and sat in red chairs while someone stood and bellowed in Italian
Perhaps this hall was used for punishment? Were wrongdoers subjected to the “tuba”? Letters found near the site marking it “The Donald J
Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts” suggest that the enormous bronze head may represent either Donald J
Kennedy, in whose joint memory the center seems to have been erected
Who were these men? They must have loved the arts
Perhaps an American Harmodius and Aristogeiton? Curiously, we do not see them commemorated jointly in other locations

Trump was in fact alive at the time of the center’s commemoration, but other scholars reply that this claim is ludicrous—where else is there evidence of a Memorial Center constructed while its subject was still living? The same theory suggests that he added his name to the center decades after its construction, halted all the shows, removed the public artworks, and threatened to demolish it if his name was not kept on, but other scholars reply that smashing things unless you can write your name on them is hardly the behavior of a full-fledged adult
We truly don’t know what to make of this place. (Just for the record, though, we didn’t do the pyramids.)

title: The Sexual Politics of the ‘Bed Trick’
excerpt: A decade ago in northern England , a young woman named Gayle Newland was convicted—twice—of an unusual crime
body: A decade ago in northern England , a young woman named Gayle Newland was convicted—twice—of an unusual crime
Another woman, who was known variously as “Chloe” and “Miss X” in court documents and media reports, reported that she’d been a victim of sexual fraud
Newland, she said, had posed as a chronically ill man named Kye Fortune in order to become her lover; the gender deception was enabled by the use of a blindfold during sex
But whenever Newland took the witness stand to testify, she shared an entirely different version of events
She and Miss X were best friends and closeted lesbians, she said, and Kye was their shared fantasy, sustained over several years

According to the British newspapers, particularly tabloids such as The Daily Mail and the Daily Express , the story was simple: Newland was a predator, carefully tricking her heterosexual friend into a lesbian relationship by pretending to be a man
The legal system and the juries affirmed this reporting, finding Newland guilty twice (the original conviction was overturned on a technicality)

Newland’s actions resembled the kind of madcap fiction in which someone pretends to be the opposite sex and hijinks ensue (as in Twelfth Night or The Rocky Horror Picture Show ); pretends to be someone’s husband in the dark (as in Chaucer’s The Canterbury Tales ); or changes sex outright, raising deeper questions (as in Virginia Woolf’s Orlando )

But Izabella Scott, whose new book, The Bed Trick , is an astoundingly well-calibrated mixture of legal reporting and literary analysis, knows full well that a heavily publicized trial is hardly the best venue for understanding other people—especially how other people have sex. “Trials are storytelling contests,” Scott writes. “They are making a case, producing stories—competitive stories that use extremes in order to win.” Scott is rightfully less interested in figuring out whether the verdict was correct (because it’s been litigated already) than in what the case illuminates about gender and truth
What preoccupies her is how the narrative device of the “bed trick,” so common in fiction and so rare in real life, came to fruition as a contest of wills between two young women

She wants to understand how two wildly disparate stories were created, what those stories tell us about ourselves, and what continues to make many people so anxious about relationships and behaviors that defy traditional norms
The Newland trials are rich texts, and Scott pores over every transcript page, looking for meaning

The case, one of sexual assault with elements of fraud, was developed in line with the U.K.’s most recent Sexual Offences Act, which was passed in 2003 and nullified consent in situations where “the defendant intentionally deceived the complainant as to the nature or purpose of the relevant act.” Scott defines this version of rape as “a violation of sexual autonomy—that is, a violation of personal freedom, of choice, and thus a violation of selfhood, identity, perhaps even humanity.” [ Read: An extraordinary account of a dangerous marriage ] Rape cases are notoriously difficult to prosecute; only a sliver of those reported (themselves a likely undercount of incidents) go to trial, and few result in a conviction
The Newland case was even more unusual , because the first conviction hinged on Section 76 of the Sexual Offences Act—the clause about deceit. (The second conviction drew on a different case, R v

McNally , which ruled that “deception as to gender can vitiate consent.”) What Miss X alleged was more complex than a simple violation of “no means no”: Because Miss X had been deceived, her yeses were built on a lie
This deception was multilayered, as Scott discovers and analyzes

Miss X came from a religious background, was estranged from her parents, and had reportedly ended an abusive relationship recently, making her especially vulnerable—whether as a closeted queer woman, as Newland attested, or as, according to Miss X, a straight woman in love with a chronically ill man whose face and body she never saw during sex
Newland first concocted the “Kye Fortune” character online at the age of 13, swiping pictures and videos from a half-Asian man named Carlo over several years
Other women reported having been duped by “Kye” online before discovering that their correspondent wasn’t a man
And after the 2017 conviction, jurors learned that Newland had also been convicted of financial fraud

But Newland stuck to her story, claiming that she and Miss X met at a gay bar, came out to each other, and shared in the “Kye” fantasy together, although they still felt compelled to stay in the closet. (The evidence for this narrative is not strong.) Newland grew up with loving parents, owned a car, and had an allowance, but she claimed that at the all-girls private school she attended, the word lesbian was a slur, conditioning her to feel lasting shame about her sexuality
She sobbed repeatedly while on the stand, even as her story wavered in its details
Scott is merciful toward Newland, affording her the benefit of the doubt that the media, and especially the legal system, couldn’t or wouldn’t

The legal acceptance of queer relationships is still a recent development, and delineating the ways in which queer sex can work—with objects and implements, with kink and other proclivities not traditionally associated with heterosexual relationships—seemed to baffle the barristers during direct questioning and cross-examination
For Scott, reading through the transcripts became an exercise in the absurd, more like Nikolai Gogol ’s “The Nose” than a typical true-crime tale

How could it not, with almost every controversial issue—race, class, queerness, gender, disability rights, consent—under the bright lights? “To read their stories is to find both” Newland and Miss X “entering a topsy-turvy world,” Scott writes, “their reason clouded by fantasy and hope, blinkered and madly doting

Both stepped over some line and their reason evaporated.” [ Read: Matt Lauer’s accuser complicates her story ] The loss of reason wasn’t exclusive to these young women, once so intimate and now such bitter adversaries
The Newland trials foreshadowed later debates about gender fluidity and sexuality, culminating in the 2025 U.K
Supreme Court ruling that the legal term woman refers to a biological woman

The Newland case featured an extreme manifestation of Britain’s cultural discomfort with shifting gender norms, but in the years since, that unease has led to decisions that are damaging the lives of many people who simply want to be left alone to be themselves
I n spite of Scott’s rigorous forensic examination of the case, it is impossible to know with certainty what happened between Newland and Miss X
Their stories diverged markedly, but that divergence remained largely consistent across the trials: two irreconcilable versions of one relationship
Scott suggests that Newland and Miss X found the plots they needed to make themselves whole, as individuals and as a couple—whether they were best friends or closeted lesbian lovers

Scott knows that she, too, is telling a story. “In my attempt to know, I construct a plot,” she writes. “In a way, this book is a shadow trial.” She writes that she is “using literary tools, like suspense and points of view,” and implores readers never to forget this
In the process, she puts storytelling itself on trial: “I think about the stories that grip us in life, but also in court
I wonder why some stories are more believable than others.” Wisely, she doesn’t offer a grand unified theory of what happened between Miss X and Newland
She knows the limits of narrative too well to do so

Still, the crime reporter in me latched on to a particular narrative contradiction, one that might point to the inciting incident that pulled the thread of deception and unraveled what was supposed to be the shared story
Newland and Miss X agree that it all fell apart one night
In Miss X’s version, “something just felt different.” Newland had insisted on oral sex; Miss X was reluctant, and the act was rough

title: Gloria Steinem’s Feminism for All
excerpt: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
body: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter
T hroughout most of Gloria Steinem’s life , two versions of her existed

Publicly, Steinem was a figurehead: the glamorous co-founder of Ms. magazine, a totem for second-wave feminism and a bull’s-eye for its detractors, gorgeously inscrutable behind her curtains of streaked hair and tinted glasses

Privately, she was a workhorse: someone who hid behind her accessories, felt she’d come to the women’s movement late (in her mid-30s), and spent much of the rest of her life hustling to make up for it
If these two identities came into conflict—the persona and the person, the superstar feminist who was terrified of public speaking—Steinem, who died yesterday at the age of 92, simply pushed on

Her politics and her life both revolved around her steadfast commitment to the idea that all women are human beings deserving of equal opportunity, and that uniting around this concept could change the world

Steinem has said she was radicalized in 1969, around her 35th birthday, when, as one of the founding journalists working for Clay Felker’s New York magazine, she covered an abortion-rights “speak-out” in Greenwich Village, where she learned that as many as one in three American women had terminated a pregnancy
The statistic shocked her, if not the procedure—a little more than a decade earlier, when Steinem was 22 and a recent Smith College graduate, she’d had one herself
Years later, the way she’d been led to cordon it off as a private incident got stuck in her brain

It was, she later wrote in her 2015 memoir, My Life on the Road , a “click of consciousness—namely, that I had been silent and silenced.” (She dedicated that book to the London doctor who had performed her abortion.) She realized that, like so many other women, she’d “been made to feel at fault, not realizing there were political reasons why female humans were not supposed to make decisions about our own bodies.” For New York , Steinem wrote a report titled “After Black Power, Women’s Liberation,” one of the first major dispatches on a national movement that was starting to take form

Steinem in Midtown Manhattan before the 1975 International Women’s Day March (Bettmann Archive / Getty) In her article, Steinem set out her thesis that for the women’s movement to be effective, it would have to be inclusive, bringing together different factions and activist groups

Throughout the 1960s, feminism had manifested most publicly as an expression of discontent among middle-class white women in the suburbs, while Black feminists worked on the fringes of the civil-rights movement and domestic workers struggled to be recognized by labor organizers
In 1963, Betty Friedan published The Feminine Mystique , a book that exposed the pervasive unhappiness of so many overeducated, underemployed housewives

By 1969, it had become clearer to many activists that forming alliances on behalf of all women might, as Steinem wrote, “forge the final revolutionary link.” Feminists were rallying around the idea that the personal is political, something Steinem knew intimately
Her mother, Ruth, had been a reporter and an editor for a newspaper in Toledo, Ohio, and her paternal grandmother had been one of the first Jewish women elected to public office in the United States
Before Steinem was born, her mother had had a nervous breakdown, and she became addicted to the chloral hydrate prescribed to her by a doctor
Her father, a traveling antiques salesman, took the family on the road for much of every year

When Steinem was roughly 10, her parents separated, and she was left to care for Ruth alone, bringing her toast and coffee while her mother lay in bed “with eyes closed and lips moving in occasional response to voices only she could hear,” as Steinem would later describe it

Steinem didn’t blame her mother for an intensely difficult childhood, seeing Ruth’s life as proof of how unequally women were suffering. [ Read: No, women aren’t the problem ] “The middle-class, educated and disillusioned group gets larger with each college graduation,” Steinem wrote in 1969
But she saw, too, that women for whom work was a need, not an opportunity, were equally deserving of representation

When she was asked to speak publicly about women’s liberation after her New York report was published, she decided to take a friend, Dorothy Pitman Hughes, with her. “Right away we discovered that a white woman and a black woman speaking together attracted far more diverse audiences than either one of us would have done on our own,” she wrote in her memoir

She formed lifelong partnerships and friendships with some of the 20th century’s most influential activists—Florynce Kennedy, Wilma Mankiller, bell hooks—and was the treasurer for the legal fund for the defense of Angela Davis
At the end of 1971, Steinem, with a collective of writers and editors, launched Ms. , a magazine that debuted as a 40-page insert tucked inside New York
The idea for a feminist publication came about during meetings when people in the movement lamented that they couldn’t get meaningful stories about women published

Brenda Feigen, who’d co-founded the Women’s Action Alliance with her, countered with the idea of a glossy magazine, a product that seemed familiar enough to appeal to women who weren’t already aligned with the cause

Even from the beginning, there were fractures between those who saw the insurgent potential of a mainstream feminist magazine and those who wanted something more radical. “We came out against marriage and motherhood,” the feminist writer Vivian Gornick said of the latter faction, in a 2011 oral history of Ms. “Gloria was uptown; we were downtown
She hung out with Establishment figures; we had only ourselves.” (Steinem pushed back later by saying that the only reason she lived uptown was that she couldn’t afford a place in the Village

She herself never had children and joked that she married in 2000, at the age of 66, only to help secure the immigration status of her husband, the entrepreneur and activist David Bale; Bale died of cancer three years later.) Steinem with some of the co-founders of Ms. magazine (Jill Krementz) The first full issue of Ms. , published in January 1972, featured an image reimagining the Hindu goddess Kali as a housewife, each of her eight arms clutching a different household item while tears stream down her face

Inside the magazine were articles on sisterhood among feminists and raising children without adhering to traditional gender roles, as well as a groundbreaking statement signed by 53 women—Steinem, Anaïs Nin, and Billie Jean King among them—noting that they had had abortions
All 300,000 printed copies sold out in eight days
Mailbags jammed with letters began arriving at the office
The magazine was broadly mocked in mainstream publications, on TV news, and even in the White House: President Richard Nixon was caught on tape deriding Steinem to Henry Kissinger
Anyone co-opted as a figurehead becomes vulnerable to charges of grandiosity, but the vitriol directed at Steinem for much of the ’70s and ’80s was almost unprecedented

In 1963, while trying to establish herself as a freelance writer, she’d worked undercover at Playboy ’s Bunny Club in Manhattan, detailing how women were subjected to internal gynecological examinations, and were routinely groped and otherwise harassed under horrific working conditions
The report caused a stir, but it also cast Steinem in many people’s minds as a lightweight who used her looks to get ahead

Because Ms. often struggled to sell ads, Steinem was obliged to fundraise for donations to keep the magazine going, appearing in public as a spokesperson for feminism in a way that galled other women in the movement

Steinem’s sphinxlike distance—she hid behind her hair, she said, because she’d always been sensitive about the roundness of her face—also fueled her detractors. “Gloria has all the irritating qualities of a saint,” Liz Smith wrote in 1971, according to Vanity Fair

By 1975, radical feminists publicly had distanced themselves from Ms. , whose politics the writer Ellen Willis described as “a mushy, sentimental idea of sisterhood designed to obscure political conflicts between women.” [ Read: The surprising tale of the bunny suit ] In her memoir, Steinem was sanguine about experiencing decades of what a Ms. article described as “trashing,” or “the dark side of sisterhood.” Needing approval, she wrote, “is a female cultural disease, and often a sign of doing the wrong thing.” What often gets obscured in any discussion of feminist infighting is the scale of what the women’s-liberation movement managed to achieve during the 1970s: landmark legal victories regarding reproductive rights, sex discrimination in the workplace, and access to education; the establishment of dozens of shelters across the country for women who were victims of domestic abuse; the passage of the Equal Rights Amendment, although it was never ratified

Betty Friedan, Elinor Guggenheimer, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Steinem at an early meeting of the National Women's Political Caucus in New York, July 19, 1971 (Don Hogan Charles / The New York Times / Redux) For Steinem, the most significant moment in her life was the 1977 National Women’s Conference in Houston, an event Steinem later described as “the most important event nobody knows about.” In 1971, she’d worked with three female representatives, Bella Abzug, Shirley Chisholm, and Patsy Mink, to establish the National Political Women’s Caucus
Now Abzug was drafting all three women to help support the unimaginable: an official platform for women in America, voted on by delegates for diverse groups from all over the country

title: The Schism Within the Trump Administration on Mexico
excerpt: Johnson tell it , the United States and Mexico have entered an era of blissful cooperation
body: Johnson tell it , the United States and Mexico have entered an era of blissful cooperation

Johnson, a former Army and intelligence officer who took up his post as U.S. ambassador to Mexico in the spring of 2025, has chronicled on his social-media feeds joint efforts to incapacitate drug cartels, tackle the screwworm pandemic, halt illegal immigration, imprison wildlife traffickers, dismantle criminal finance networks, and expand soybean exports

For Johnson, the U.S. – Mexico relationship is defined by “close coordination,” “decisive action,” “information shared,” and “the security of both our nations.” His hashtag of choice is #TogetherWeAchieveMore
Johnson’s Mexico is one in which the country’s security chief, nicknamed Batman, has made remarkable strides against criminal networks
Other members of the Trump administration see things differently
Stephen Miller’s Mexico has a cartel-dominated government that has obstinately refused to cooperate in the fight against drugs and illegal immigration
It’s a place where terrorist organizations “kill, extort, kidnap, or murder anybody who gets in their way,” as he said in a July speech
Miller’s Mexico is one in which the U.S. military might need to do what an ineffectual Mexican government cannot
Perhaps no other bilateral relationship has exposed so publicly the stark disconnects within the Trump administration
Mexican officials say they have become accustomed to bipolarity—a “ doble discurso ,” they call it—in their interactions with the U.S. government
Some meetings suggest that things are going swimmingly

Others seem to telegraph the possibility of an American air strike. “Sometimes they say one thing, and other times they say another” was how Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum explained the vacillation during a press conference in August

Last week, after Johnson’s run of public praise, U.S. officials revived a periodic critique against Mexico in meetings in Washington between Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Mexican foreign minister, Roberto Velasco: Mexico isn’t doing enough to stop its own citizens from migrating to the United States
More than half of the people apprehended by U.S
U.S. officials asked why Mexico couldn’t halt the flow of its own citizens
To Mexican officials, it felt like an unfair demand, given how much they had already offered the U.S. on immigration enforcement
Although overall apprehensions at the U.S.-Mexico border are up slightly from last year, they are down roughly 90 percent from 2023, thanks in part to Mexican cooperation
And although Mexican authorities have made it much more difficult for migrants from other countries to approach the border, deterring Mexicans presents a different sort of challenge

Detaining Mexicans moving through their own country “would be a violation of Mexican law,” the country’s former immigration chief Tonatiuh Guillén López told us. “It would pin the state against its own citizens.” Johnson had posted on X that the Rubio meeting “reflects our commitment to work together to stop illegal migration.” But the secretary’s office struck a different tone, suggesting that Rubio wasn’t satisfied with what he had heard

Rubio, a post-meeting readout from the department explained, had “called for decisive action to end illegal immigration, stop the trafficking of fentanyl and other illicit drugs into the United States, and dismantle foreign terrorist organizations and cartels and deprive them of arms.” Asked about the inconsistency in messaging about Mexico, the White House echoed Miller’s sentiments. “As President Trump has said, and as the U.S. government has repeatedly and clearly communicated, it is unacceptable that foreign terrorist organizations control vast territories across Mexico, including the entire region that directly borders the United States,” the White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told us in a statement
The United States’ most important trade agreement could get caught in the tug-of-war over whether Mexico is doing enough to further U.S. interests

As the United States, Mexico, and Canada work through the annual review of the trilateral USMCA trade deal, Miller has privately floated the possibility that the U.S. could use the occasion to pressure Mexico into doing more on immigration enforcement, one U.S. official said
Although the focus of the USMCA review has been more on granular disputes over supply chains and the origins of raw materials, the U.S. could decide to withdraw from the deal entirely
If that happened, the economic blow to all three countries would be substantial
U .S. law-enforcement officials based in Mexico gush about the kind of close security coordination that they’re seeing now, but that hadn’t existed for more than a decade

Since Sheinbaum’s election in 2024, Mexico has acted on U.S. intelligence to take down top cartel leaders; it has extradited more than 100 alleged criminals to the United States; it has detained thousands of migrants en route to the U.S. border and permitted thousands of non-Mexican deportees from the U.S. to be sent to southern Mexico

Sheinbaum’s predecessor openly considered stripping Drug Enforcement Administration agents of diplomatic immunity; now those agents have supported a series of major security operations. [ Read: A reverse Ellis Island ] “On security cooperation, what we’ve seen is a massive improvement under Sheinbaum
We’re getting things that were blocked for years—from extraditions to action against cartels,” one recently retired U.S. official who had been based in Mexico told us
But for another group of U.S. officials, those actions are grossly insufficient
Miller in particular has lobbied for unilateral U.S. action against Mexican cartels
When he meets with Mexican officials, he typically complains about the country’s inaction
During Fox News interviews, he has used Mexico City, along with Baghdad, as examples of the world’s most dangerous cities

Sheinbaum has responded by saying she asked her foreign minister to send “this White House official the data concerning Mexico City, which perhaps he is not aware of.” (Mexico City has roughly the same homicide rate as Portland, Oregon.) In recent weeks, U.S. diplomatic and trade officials have grown worried that the USMCA, negotiated during Trump’s first term, could be blown up if some of the president’s advisers get their way
U.S.-Canada relations are already strained over bilateral disputes; now negotiators fear that the broader pact could become a casualty of Trump’s immigration and cartel crackdowns
Peter Navarro, a senior adviser to Trump on trade and manufacturing, has cast doubt on the deal, arguing that it needs major changes or should be scrapped altogether
Mexico is the United States’ largest trading partner—another point that Johnson makes frequently, but something that Navarro and other members of the Trump administration seem to view as a liability
The deal enables a regional supply chain in which parts of a final product are sourced and assembled across the three countries
If the USMCA were to be abandoned or weakened, manufacturing costs throughout North America would rise dramatically
But the stakes of any USMCA renegotiation go well beyond the future of a trade pact

If the administration uses the deal to gain leverage over immigration and security policy, it would blur the line between trade policy and national security, and put the basic rules governing North American commerce at the mercy of disputes far outside trade

title: The Download: rethinking child safety and fossil-fueled farming

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
Child-monitoring apps might need a reboot Digital harms have become the defining fear of American parents

In response, they’re increasingly turning to content-monitoring apps that scan their children’s texts, photos, emails, and chats, issuing alerts whenever an algorithm flags something it deems dangerous
These tools have had genuine successes, preventing suicide attempts, intercepting predators, and averting school shootings
But they can also cause harm themselves, from false alarms and unnecessary interventions to damaged trust and anxiety
Child-safety researchers say better approaches exist
Here’s what they think those could look like . —Kelly Clancy This article is from our latest print magazine, which is all about kids

The war in Iran has pushed natural-gas prices higher and disrupted fertilizer trade through the Strait of Hormuz—and its closure could make access harder still for some of the world’s poorest countries

Let’s take a closer look at the surging fertilizer prices, and how a few climate-friendly alternatives could bring farmers some relief . —Casey Crownhart This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter

title: Agriculture relies on fossil fuels. It’s costing us.
excerpt: Fertilizer prices are on a wild ride : The war in Iran has sent fertilizer costs soaring — urea (the most commonly applied fertilizer) hit $850 per metric ton i
body: Fertilizer prices are on a wild ride : The war in Iran has sent fertilizer costs soaring — urea (the most commonly applied fertilizer) hit $850 per metric ton in April, 80% higher than pre-conflict levels
Prices have come down somewhat but could stay elevated through 2028
The fossil fuel problem runs deep : Natural gas isn't just used to power fertilizer production — it's a core chemical ingredient, meaning every energy price spike hits farmers

Microbes might offer some relief : Companies like Pivot Bio and Switch Bioworks are using genetically edited microbes to partly replace synthetic fertilizers — and unlike chemical alternatives, their prices don't swing with natural gas markets. " data-chronoton-post-id="1143320" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> If you’ve had to fill up your vehicle’s gas tank or buy a plane ticket lately, you’ve probably felt the effects of rising fossil-fuel prices
But farmers buying fertilizer for their crops are especially aware of just how far the ripple effects of the conflict in Iran have spread
Fertilizer prices have been on a roller coaster this year, kicked off in part by trade disruptions and high prices for natural gas, a key ingredient in fertilizer production
Let’s take a closer look at why conventional fertilizer prices are so sky-high, and how a few more climate-friendly alternatives could bring farmers some relief
As fossil-fuel prices go up, nearly all industries are affected, since most of our economy relies on these fuels to move goods and people around
But fertilizer is even more intertwined with these fluctuations, because natural gas is used as both an energy source and a chemical input in the production of ammonia, a key fertilizer ingredient

So as natural-gas prices have spiked in recent months because of the war in Iran, fertilizer prices have followed . (It’s worth briefly noting here that fertilizer production is also a major source of greenhouse-gas emissions, accounting for about 2% of the global total.) Fertilizer trade is being directly affected as well, since about one-third of global seaborne trade in fertilizers passes through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed to commercial traffic because of the conflict
Access to fertilizer could get worse for some of the poorest countries around the world because of the strait’s closure, according to a report from the World Bank
While the US largely meets demand for nitrogen fertilizers with domestic production, some imports do come from the Persian Gulf
At one point in April, the price of urea (the most commonly applied fertilizer) climbed above $850 per metric ton
That’s 80% higher than it was before the conflict and the highest level since 2022, when the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the resulting conflict caused fertilizer costs to hit record highs

Prices have come down significantly, but forecasts remain uncertain. “There’s just this out-of-control supply chain that’s a lot more volatile than it’s ever been,” says Travis Frey, chief technology officer of Pivot Bio, a company making fertilizer with genetically edited microbes. (For more on these microbes, how they work, and what research is still needed, check out my latest story here .) Pivot says its products are cost-competitive with chemical fertilizers today
And because they don’t use natural gas as an input, they aren’t subject to the same price spikes
When the war in Iran started, Pivot increased the volume it planned to produce, dropped prices, and allowed farmers to lock in prices for three years, Frey says
That could be a major help for those farmers, because high prices could be here to stay for a while
Some fertilizer prices could remain high through at least 2028, according to a report from CoBank, one of the largest banks for the agriculture industry in the US
That’s partly because the war has caused long-lasting damage: 31 ammonia plants in the Middle East have been affected or shut down completely
That’s on top of 20 ammonia plants that have been damaged in Russia in recent years

Ongoing high prices can be extremely challenging for farmers. “The fertilizer price spikes, and because farmers have paper-thin margins, this is a real problem,” says Tim Schnabel, founder and CEO of Switch Bioworks, another company working on advanced microbe fertilizers
Higher costs can help push food prices higher, causing all of us to pay more at the grocery store. (It’s not just fertilizer, by the way
Farmers are also getting hit with wild diesel prices this year.) As long as we’re relying on fertilizers made with fossil fuels, food prices will be tied up with energy prices
Switch and Pivot are among the companies looking to make alternative fertilizers that use microbes to provide nitrogen to plants

There’s a limit to how much synthetic fertilizers these products can actually replace: Depending on the crop and conditions, Pivot says, its products can replace about 25% of synthetic fertilizer today, and the company hopes to reach 40% to 50% of the total

But these alternatives could be a start to untangling fossil fuels and food. “We can’t keep doing it like this,” Switch’s Schnabel says. “There’s no way we can build a society where the basis of the food chain depends on fossil fuels.” This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: Scaling agentic AI pilots across the enterprise
excerpt: As agentic AI moves from experimentation toward enterprise deployment, the challenge is figuring out how agents can work together, connect to the systems and da
body: As agentic AI moves from experimentation toward enterprise deployment, the challenge is figuring out how agents can work together, connect to the systems and data they need, and operate safely across the workflows that run a business
Although agentic AI has been adopted by some 80% of Fortune 500 companies, progress toward meaningful scale remains uneven, with many organizations still working through isolated pilots

WATCH THE WEBCAST For Arun Chandra, chief operating officer at NiCE, the first step is moving beyond experimentation for its own sake. “Everybody’s trying to figure out what can we do with this technology?” he says

But scaling requires a clearer connection to business strategy: Organizations need to define whether they are trying to increase revenue, reduce costs, or pursue another strategic or financial objective

From there, they need to rethink the workflows where agents will operate instead of just layering AI onto existing processes. “The last thing you want to do is to apply AI on an outdated or an inefficient workflow,” Chandra says
That shift requires organizations to treat agentic AI as a cohesive system
Agents need access to the data, knowledge, and context required to make effective decisions, as well as connections to back-end systems if they are expected to take action
Fragmented information can undermine those capabilities: “The efficacy of these AI agents is purely a function of the context, the knowledge, and the data they can ingest and use,” Chandra says
The organizational implications are equally noteworthy

Scaling agents can create a new form of fragmentation if teams build isolated systems that don’t connect with one another, while governance, privacy, security, and change management become more important as agents take on more consequential work
Chandra argues that AI agents should ultimately be held to the same standards as human workers, with organizations thinking of their workforce as a combination of humans and AI agents
Looking ahead, that connected approach could enable agents to work proactively and even communicate with other agents to resolve customer needs

For organizations making the transition from pilots to scale, the priority is not to “boil the ocean,” Chandra says, but to instead build a connected strategy around high-value use cases, workflows, workforce changes, and measurable outcomes

title: What we forget when we remember 9/11
url:
<title>What we forget when we remember 9/11</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757830/original/file-20260903-50-2xuirc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8192%2C5461&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">&#39;No Day Shall Erase You From the Memory of Time,&#39; a phrase written by the Roman poet Virgil, is displayed on a wall at the 9/11 Memorial Museum.  </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/workers-clean-a-wall-at-the-9-11-memorial-museum-as-it-news-photo/2293034775?adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>For much of the past 25 years, each anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks has arrived with signs and stickers reminding people to “<a href="https://t2t.org/9-11-never-forget/">never forget</a>.”</p>

<p>I have always felt unsure about what those words mean. For those of us who were alive in 2001, forgetting the day itself is almost impossible. </p>

<p>I remember the shock and fear, <a href="https://www.c-span.org/clip/public-affairs-event/user-clip-9-11-2nd-plane-hitting-world-trade-center/4767841">the replays of the second plane hitting the World Trade Center</a>, and the moment <a href="https://www.c-span.org/clip/call-in/user-clip-the-second-tower-collapses/4513795">the second tower fell</a>. I remember seeing on television the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TmBKJGLawUY">missing-person photographs that covered New York</a> and the awful recognition that very few of those people were likely to be found alive. I remember the <a href="https://www.hks.harvard.edu/more/hks-magazine/twenty-five-years-after-911-first-battalion-chief-send-firefighters-twin-towers">bravery of the New York firefighters and police</a>.</p>

<p>My college students have no such memories or feelings. Most were born years after Sept. 11, 2001.</p>

<p>They encounter what happened through photographs, documentaries, memorials, classroom lessons and stories told by people who were alive on that day. The National September 11 Memorial &amp; Museum estimates that <a href="https://911memorial.org/news-release-911-memorial-museum-launches-new-campaign-educate-and-inspire">about 100 million Americans have been born since the attacks</a>.</p>

<p>The shift is ordinary and still somehow startling. An event that once felt like it had <a href="https://www.doomsdayscenario.co/p/17-minutes">split time into a permanent before and after</a> is fading into history itself.</p>

<p>In my <a href="https://experts.boisestate.edu/en/persons/stephanie-martin/">work as a professor</a> of politics and public affairs, I pay close attention to the stories Americans tell about their past and the ways those stories shape civic identity in the present. The 25th anniversary of 9/11 is especially interesting to me because it marks a moment when an event once experienced as immediate and world-changing is increasingly being carried forward through memory, ritual and interpretation.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<h2>Understanding history includes forgetting</h2>

<p>Scholars of collective memory, also called public memory, <a href="https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev.soc.24.1.105">have long argued</a> that societies do not remember the past simply by preserving it.</p>

<p>Public memory describes how collective meaning gets made and remade through stories, institutions, rituals and political arguments. For example, <a href="https://www.oig.dhs.gov/node/7203">the Department of Homeland Security was created in response to 9/11</a>. Many Americans understand DHS as a structural and cultural reform made to fix the <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/9-11-and-the-reinvention-of-the-u-s-intelligence-community/">intelligence failures that the attacks made evident</a>.</p>

<p>Forgetting is part of the process, too. As <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1750698007083889">memory scholar Paul Connerton has argued</a>, some forms of forgetting are not failures but necessary parts of social life. </p>

<p>No individual, school or nation can keep everything equally present forever. History accumulates faster than collective memory can accommodate it. The question, then, is not whether Americans will forget parts of 9/11. They will. The more interesting question is what remains after that forgetting takes place.</p>

<p>From the first anniversary, commemorating the attacks has carried a careful choreography. There is the <a href="https://www.911memorial.org/plan-your-own-911-anniversary-observance">annual reading of the names of those who died, the memorial lights and the stories of first responders</a>, each of which keeps the human loss and courage of the day in view. </p>

<p>In a <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2016/12/15/americans-name-the-10-most-significant-historic-events-of-their-lifetimes/">2016 Pew Research Center survey</a>, 76% of Americans named 9/11 as one of the 10 most consequential events of their lifetimes. Nearly 1 in 5 said the nation’s immediate response to the attacks was the moment when they <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2017/09/11/about-a-fifth-of-americans-cite-911-response-as-event-that-made-them-most-proud-of-u-s/">felt most proud of the United States</a>.</p>

<p>I understand those points of view. Some of what I most want preserved about Sept. 11 is the shared grief of those first days and the ways ordinary people revealed their humanity under unimaginable circumstances. </p>

<p>Firefighters climbed stairs and ran toward mortal danger, while a cascade of people tried as hard as they could to get down. Office workers helped colleagues and strangers. Families searched for missing loved ones long after hope had become terribly thin. And <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/United-Airlines-flight-93">passengers on United Flight 93 fought back</a> and forced the plane they were on to crash in a field in the middle of Philadelphia, sacrificing themselves in the hopes of saving others.</p>

<p>Before 9/11 became a justification, a policy, a war or a political symbol, it was an experience of shared human vulnerability.</p>

<h2>Politics and its consequences</h2>

<p>No event remains sealed inside its original meaning. Sept. 11 became the starting point for a series of political choices that reshaped American life and, in turn, reshaped the memory of the day itself. </p>

<p>The attacks led to <a href="https://www.9-11commission.gov/report/911Report.pdf">the war in Afghanistan</a>, which lasted for 20 years after the invasion’s initial success in dismantling al-Qaida and removing the Taliban government. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.9-11commission.gov/report/911Report.pdf">Next was the invasion of Iraq</a>, even though Saddam Hussein’s regime had no role in 9/11. </p>

<p>And the aftermath of the attacks helped create an atmosphere that allowed for <a href="https://purl.stanford.edu/nd865mg8547">expanding government surveillance</a>, <a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/R/PDF/R43983/R43983.3.pdf">enlarging presidential power</a> and <a href="https://www.aclu.org/documents/freedom-under-fire-dissent-post-911-america">narrowing the space for dissent</a>. Muslim Americans found themselves subjected to <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/the-american-public-on-the-911-decade-a-study-of-american-public-opinion/">new suspicion and hostility</a>. </p>

<p>Those consequences now compete with the original experience of Sept. 11 for <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2021/09/02/two-decades-later-the-enduring-legacy-of-9-11/">a place in its meaning</a>. </p>

<p>For some Americans, the attacks have become inseparable from the wars and broader <a href="https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/commission-civil-rights-examines-freedom-post-911-aclu-says-fears-setting-public">official willingness to sacrifice civil liberties in the name of security</a> that followed. From this perspective, 9/11 is remembered not only as a national trauma but also as a warning about how fear and grief can make <a href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/lessons-learned-u-s-national-security-policy-20-years-since-911/">policies that once seemed unthinkable appear necessary</a>.</p>

<p>For others, the day – and its aftermath – represent restored American pride and military perseverance. </p>

<p>For still others, 9/11 remains most powerfully a story about innocent lives lost and ordinary people behaving with extraordinary courage. </p>

<p>Each way of remembering draws a boundary around the terrorism the nation experienced, deciding how far beyond that September morning its meaning should extend.</p>

<p>Even events once regarded as world-defining eventually have to share the historical landscape with everything that follows. Since 2001, Americans have experienced <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/topic/subject/hurricane-katrina">Hurricane Katrina</a>, <a href="https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/great-recession-of-200709">the 2008 financial crisis</a>, <a href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/presidential-documents-archive-guidebook/documents-related-presidential-elections/2008">the election of the first Black president</a>, the <a href="https://millercenter.org/president/trump/campaigns-and-elections">rise of Donald Trump</a>, the <a href="https://www.loc.gov/collections/january-6th-attack-on-the-us-capitol-web-archive/about-this-collection/">violence on Jan. 6, 2021</a>, and a <a href="https://www.loc.gov/collections/coronavirus-web-archive/about-this-collection/">global pandemic</a>. </p>

<p>Sept. 11 has not become unimportant because those things happened. Its place in the story has changed because life – because the world – kept going.</p>

<p>For people who were alive during the attacks, there is something sad about watching that distance and diminishment happen. When an event once remembered in minute detail becomes a date others know only from history, the passage of one’s own life becomes newly visible. There is a strange nostalgia in realizing that something once so immediate now belongs increasingly to people who know it only as the past.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What are we to remember?</h2>

<p>Maybe this is why “never forget” feels both moving and impossible.</p>

<p>What is supposed to be the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2021/09/08/nyregion/9-11-new-york-remember.html">subject of our remembering</a>? The people who died? The courage? The grief? The fear? The wars that followed? The mistakes? The unexpected decency of people thrown together on an unbearable day?</p>

<p>A society cannot keep all of those things equally vivid forever. Nor should its members confuse remembering everything with understanding anything. The task of collective memory is <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2352250X17302592">inevitably one of selection</a>.</p>

<p>For me, one part of the memory seems especially important to preserve. Before Sept. 11 became an argument about war, security, patriotism or political allegiance, it was an encounter with human vulnerability and then human resilience. The solidarity of Sept. 11 and the political choices made in its aftermath were not the same thing, even if they have become intertwined in our memory of the period.</p>

<p>If the ongoing march of history means Sept. 11 cannot always carry the emotional weight it does for people who were alive when it happened, perhaps the best outcome would be to focus on the collective grief, along with the extraordinary human response that grief engendered. </p>

<p>Doing so would not erase any of what followed. But it might help preserve the understanding that the day was one of imaginable horror and tragedy before it became a political inheritance.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290418/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Hiking canyons can quickly turn deadly when storms hit – what you should know before going in</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757808/original/file-20260903-50-bhhnhf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3936%2C2624&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Mud and debris, including a mangled piece of construction equipment, remain after a flash flood in Grand Canyon National Park on Aug. 31, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/GrandCanyonFlooding/cab0255182f64d2aaa6e01f09e54089c/photo?vs=false&amp;currentItemNo=38&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">Katherine Hensel/National Park Service via AP</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Hiking a picturesque valley or climbing a craggy gorge are some of the most exhilarating experiences in nature. As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=39NGsnIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">geologist</a>, I have hiked and climbed some of the most intense terrains in the world, including in the Andes, Middle Eastern deserts, the Balkans and the Appalachians.</p>

<p>I am particularly drawn to canyons that provide beautiful windows into the rock record and the geologic history of a place. However, these narrow valleys can quickly become extremely dangerous when water pours in.</p>

<p>At Grand Canyon National Park in Arizona, at least two hikers died and a third was missing after <a href="https://www.adn.com/nation-world/2026/08/31/more-storms-possible-at-grand-canyon-where-a-flash-flood-killed-1-person-and-left-15-missing/">powerful monsoon storms sent</a> a deluge into one of the narrowest parts of the canyon on Aug. 29, 2026. Two of the survivors who were rescued described seeing the water quickly rise over the trail as they <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/weather/2026/09/02/deep-grand-canyon-rain-left-them-nowhere-go/">clung to a ledge</a>, fearing they might never see their families again.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757799/original/file-20260903-70-mq66he.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People stand on the rim of the Grand Canyon as a storm moves through." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757799/original/file-20260903-70-mq66he.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757799/original/file-20260903-70-mq66he.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757799/original/file-20260903-70-mq66he.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757799/original/file-20260903-70-mq66he.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757799/original/file-20260903-70-mq66he.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757799/original/file-20260903-70-mq66he.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757799/original/file-20260903-70-mq66he.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>So, how do you balance a love for outdoor activity with managing this risk and hike canyons safely?</p>

<h2>Why canyons are prone to flash floods</h2>

<p>To understand the dynamics of a flash flood, it helps to start with the geomorphologic aspect – understanding the landforms and how they change over time.</p>

<p>In canyons and <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/arroyo">arroyos</a> – steep gullies common to the Southwest – flash flooding can occur even when the heavy rainfall happens great distances away. A person can be hiking under clear skies in the canyon and not be aware that heavy rain falling upstream or even outside of the canyon means a disaster is unfolding.</p>

<p>The steep gradients and narrow passageways that define these landscapes channel the water, sending vast amounts of it rushing downstream. Under these conditions, water can rise quickly in the narrow space of a canyon.</p>



<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757872/original/file-20260903-50-kdo1w3.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Timelapse images of the radar shows strong storms upstream and over Bright Angel Canyon ahead of the flood." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757872/original/file-20260903-50-kdo1w3.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757872/original/file-20260903-50-kdo1w3.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757872/original/file-20260903-50-kdo1w3.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757872/original/file-20260903-50-kdo1w3.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757872/original/file-20260903-50-kdo1w3.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757872/original/file-20260903-50-kdo1w3.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757872/original/file-20260903-50-kdo1w3.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Time-lapse radar shows the storms moving over the regions of the Grand Canyon where the flood hit, near Phantom Ranch.</span>
