<p>The Grand Canyon flood involved heavy downpours in the <a href="https://azstateparks.com/monsoon-season-in-arizona">heart of monsoon season</a>. The intensity of the rainfall matters in a canyon. Even in arid regions, which generally get low amounts of rain annually, heavy rainfall within a short period of time can create devastating floods.</p>

<p>In 2018, a <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-43912019">flash flood in Israel’s Tzafit Canyon</a> – an environment similar to the part of the Grand Canyon where the 2026 flood occurred – claimed the lives of 10 recent high school graduates who were hiking in the canyon. </p>

<p>I grew up in that region and had hiked there many times, and I remember thinking about the incomprehensible suddenness: One moment you are appreciating the breathtaking views of the desert, and within minutes you are fighting a torrent of water you never imagined in such an arid place. A <a href="https://nhess.copernicus.org/articles/21/1583/2021/">year’s worth of rain</a> fell near the canyon that day.</p>

<h2>The hydrogeologic aspect</h2>

<p>How well the ground absorbs water also affects flood dynamics. Soils that are highly <a href="https://waterportal.ca/learn-how-water-flows-underground-recharge-permeability-and-porosity/">porous and permeable</a> can transmit water easily vertically into the ground.</p>

<p>However, in arid regions such as Arizona and the <a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-21-1583-2021">Negev Desert</a>, where Tzafit Canyon lies, the dry ground tends to form hardened crusts that make it harder for the water to sink in. That exacerbates surface flooding.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757797/original/file-20260903-60-huzhd3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two people wait on a rocky canyon floor for a helicopter in the distance." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757797/original/file-20260903-60-huzhd3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757797/original/file-20260903-60-huzhd3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757797/original/file-20260903-60-huzhd3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757797/original/file-20260903-60-huzhd3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757797/original/file-20260903-60-huzhd3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757797/original/file-20260903-60-huzhd3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757797/original/file-20260903-60-huzhd3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Dozens of people were evacuated by helicopter from the canyon after the flood.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Grand%20Canyon%20Flooding/68a5f65c69ba4a079823cfa379a389fb/photo">Katherine Hensel/National Park Service via AP</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>What’s more, the lack of vegetation in dry and rocky environments means that water can flow more rapidly down slopes.</p>

<h2>What should hikers do to stay safe?</h2>

<p>As an avid hiker, I value the beauty of nature and geology that canyons offer, and I believe in enjoying them. However, it is important to understand the risks and to prepare before hiking, climbing or backpacking in these areas.</p>

<p>Carefully study your environment before going in, so you know the risks and the escape routes that will let you get to safety in the event of a flash flood.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757892/original/file-20260903-50-v095wn.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An elevation map of the area where the flood happened shows the steepness" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757892/original/file-20260903-50-v095wn.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757892/original/file-20260903-50-v095wn.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=464&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757892/original/file-20260903-50-v095wn.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=464&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757892/original/file-20260903-50-v095wn.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=464&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757892/original/file-20260903-50-v095wn.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=583&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757892/original/file-20260903-50-v095wn.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=583&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757892/original/file-20260903-50-v095wn.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=583&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">An elevation map of the Grand Canyon shows how narrow and steep it is, with 1,500-meter drop over an area less than 5 miles. The white dot shows the location where people were rescued from the flood on Aug. 29, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://databasin.org/datasets/3cf598b2d67b4f9f8e3ff47fd5b5ae37/">Anner Paldor; Data Basin, using ESRI, Census Bureau, NOAA, National Ocean Service, National Geodetic Survey, USGS, TomTom</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Gear up properly. Prepare for your trip so you have the equipment you need. Make sure you have a flashlight with extra batteries, a whistle to signal first responders, and extra clothes in case you get wet. If you know you will be hiking in high-risk water zones, you may consider an inflatable personal flotation device. </p>

<p>Talk to park rangers before going in so you know the current conditions and so someone knows where you’re going.</p>

<p>Always be aware of the weather – not just above you but upstream. Clear skies can be deceptive. An added challenge is that cellular service is often shaky in deep canyons and remote areas. Check the weather forecast before you go down a canyon, not just for the specific location, but also for the surrounding area. The <a href="https://www.weather.gov/">National Weather Service</a> provides warnings of flash floods and other extreme weather events.</p>

<p>When you are in a canyon, a good general guideline is to try to stay as high as possible and to be alert to the sound of an incoming flood. One person described the rush of water in the Grand Canyon <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/rep-david-schweikert-describes-surviving-deadly-grand-canyon-flash-flo-rcna595625">sounding like a freight train</a>.  </p>

<p>If heavy rain starts, use extra caution and seek higher ground. Be aware that the timing of floods can vary widely – scientists analyzed 74,814 flash flood events in the U.S. and found the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.124106">average duration was around 3½ hours</a>, but some persisted for more than 48 hours. A flood can start quickly and strand people for long periods of time. <a href="https://www.facebook.com/Denver7News/videos/dramatic-footage-from-a-hiker-as-they-sought-safety-during-flooding-in-the-grand/1037507952609760/">Muddy water or debris in a normally clear stream</a> are two signs of flooding developing. Rising water or the distant sound of rushing water is another clear warning to get to safety fast.</p>

<p>There are always risks in nature, but that does not mean you should avoid being out in nature. Planning ahead and hiking with caution and awareness can help you enjoy the beautiful outdoors and come back home safely.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291122/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Qué hacer si se impugna tu voto: consejos prácticos para las elecciones de mitad de legislatura</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757545/original/file-20260827-60-uedg3o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8192%2C5461&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Muchos estados permiten inscribirse el mismo día en el colegio electoral.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/empty-voting-booths-on-election-day-royalty-free-image/1401415073?phrase=midterm+elections">adamkaz/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Ahora que las <a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/us-midterms-129216">elecciones de mitad de legislatura de 2026</a> entran en su recta final, es importante que conozcas tus derechos por si se impugna tu voto.  </p>

<p>La mejor manera de asegurarte de que tu voto se tenga en cuenta es defender tus propios intereses. Soy abogada y profesor de la iniciativa de defensa de los derechos civiles para estudiantes universitarios de <a href="https://dornsife.usc.edu/profile/karen-figueroa-clewett">la Universidad del Sur de California</a>, Agents of Change. A continuación te indico varias formas sencillas de asegurarte de que tu voto se cuente y dos soluciones prácticas que puedes considerar si tu voto sigue siendo objeto de impugnación. </p>

<p>Una parte fundamental para asegurarte de que puedas votar consiste en realizar los preparativos necesarios antes incluso de llegar al colegio electoral. Sigue leyendo para saber cómo y dónde inscribirte, dónde y cuándo puedes votar, y a qué números llamar si necesitas información que no encuentres en Internet.</p>

<h2>¿Está registrado para votar? Confírmelo</h2>

<p>Antes de votar, debe asegurarse de que está  registrado para votar. Puede verificar el estatus de su registro utilizando esta <a href="https://www.usvotefoundation.org/am-i-registered">herramienta en línea</a>. Si no puede usar una herramienta en línea, llame a su oficina electoral local o a una línea de ayuda para votantes como las que se enumeran en una  sección a continuación. </p>

<p>Si se da cuenta de que no está registrado, puede usar <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/electronic-or-online-voter-registration.aspx#Table%20of%20states%20w/ovr">esta herramienta</a> de la Conferencia Nacional de Legislaturas Estatales para encontrar la solicitud de registro en línea de su estado. Si necesita hacer esto en persona, llame a su oficina electoral local para recibir instrucciones.</p>

<p>Para este momento, es posible que ya haya pasado la fecha límite para el registro de votantes en su estado. Pero puede que no sea demasiado tarde para que se registre. </p>

<p>Muchos estados permiten el registro el mismo día en el sitio de votación. Puede encontrar las leyes de su estado sobre el día de la votación detalladas <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/same-day-registration.aspx">aquí</a>. Pídale al trabajador electoral, en el  centro de votación que le corresponda, un formulario de registro para el mismo día; complete el formulario y luego solicite una “boleta condicional”. Una boleta condicional permite a los funcionarios electorales contabilizar su voto después de verificar su elegibilidad como votante. Si no puede buscar en línea, puede llamar a su oficina electoral local para averiguar si puede registrarse el mismo día de las elecciones.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Tres jóvenes con mochilas, hablando; uno de ellos está leyendo algo en un portapapeles que sostiene en la mano." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/621131/original/file-20240923-20-l117du.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">Marchellos Scott, a la derecha, ayuda a los estudiantes del Morehouse College a rellenar un formulario de inscripción en el censo electoral en un puesto de inscripción de la universidad el 19 de agosto de 2024, en Atlanta.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/marchellos-scott-helps-morehouse-college-students-fill-out-news-photo/2168355994?adppopup=true">Elijah Nouvelage/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Reúna los documentos para verificar su identidad</h2>

<p>Las leyes de identificación de votantes generalmente se refieren a la votación en persona, no las boletas en ausencia ni las boletas enviadas por correo.</p>

<p>Si vive en un estado que requiere verificar la identidad para el voto en persona, reúna los documentos requeridos, que pueden variar desde licencias de conducir hasta estados de cuenta bancarios con información de identificación, antes de dirigirse  al lugar de votación que le corresponda. Puede encontrar la información de contacto de la oficina electoral de su condado <a href="https://www.usvotefoundation.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm">aquí</a>. Esta <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/voter-id.aspx">página web</a>  incluye una tabla que enumera los documentos de identificación aceptables de cada estado y las posibles excepciones para algunas personas. También puede llamar a su oficina electoral local para averiguar qué se requiere.</p>

<p>Votantes ausentes: Localice las normas de verificación de identidad de su estado <a href="https://www.vote.org/voter-id-laws/">aquí</a>.</p>

<h2>Encuentre el lugar de votación correcto</h2>

<p>Puede asegurarse de que se dirige al lugar de votación correcto con esta <a href="https://www.vote.org/polling-place-locator/">herramienta</a>. O llame a la oficina electoral de su condado para encontrar el centro  de votación que le corresponde y su horario de operación; puede buscar la información de contacto de la oficina electoral de su condado <a href="https://www.usvotefoundation.org/vote/eoddomestic.htm">aquí</a>.</p>

<p>Una vez que sepa cuál es su lugar de votación y su horario, puede ir allí y registrarse. En la mayoría de los casos, se le entregará una boleta, se le mostrará dónde votar y se le pedirá que deposite su boleta en una máquina o una urna, luego de lo cual podrá continuar alegremente con su vida. </p>

<p>Es en el momento del registro donde las cosas pueden salir mal.</p>

<h2>Problemas en su centro de votación</h2>

<p>Aquí se presentan posibles problemas al momento de votar y formas de solucionarlos.</p>

<p>Posibilidad #1: Máquinas de votación descompuestas. </p>

<p>Si le piden que se vaya debido a que las máquinas se descompusieron, no se vaya. Pida que le den una boleta de papel.</p>

<p>Posibilidad #2: Está esperando en la fila y los funcionarios informan que el centro de votación ha cerrado.</p>

<p>Si llego a la fila del centro de votación antes de que cerrara, no permita que lo rechacen a la hora del cierre si no ha votado. Tiene el derecho legal de votar en esas circunstancias, <a href="https://www.vote.org/election-protection/">así que permanezca en la fila y espere para emitir su voto</a>.</p>

<p>Posibilidad #3: No está en la lista de votantes registrados.</p>

<p>Si le dicen que no puede votar porque su nombre no está en la lista de votantes, <a href="https://www.aclu.org/know-your-rights/voting-rights#what-are-my-general-rights-on-election-day">pídale al trabajador del sitio de votación que verifique nuevamente</a> y que revise  la lista de votantes suplementarios. Si aún no logran encontrar su nombre, pídale al trabajador electoral que verifique si usted se encuentra en el lugar correcto.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Tres personas sentadas frente a las pantallas de sus ordenadores en una mesa cubierta con un mantel negro" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=8%2C8%2C5982%2C3979&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/492849/original/file-20221101-26796-z7ho0z.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Posibilidad #4: Alguien dice que no tiene derecho a votar.</p>

<p>Si su elegibilidad para votar sigue siendo cuestionada pese a que está seguro de estar en el lugar de votación correcto, <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/provisional-ballots.aspx">solicite emitir un voto provisional</a>, que está disponible en todos los estados, excepto en Idaho y Minnesota. Puede encontrar detalles sobre las reglas de votación provisional de su estado <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/research/elections-and-campaigns/provisional-ballots.aspx">aquí</a>.</p>

<p>Haga un seguimiento de su boleta provisional <a href="https://www.vote.org/ballot-tracker-tools/">aquí</a>.</p>

<h2>Llame a una línea de ayuda</h2>

<p>Si no recibe una boleta provisional, llame a una línea de ayuda para obtener asistencia  electoral. Aquí hay cuatro líneas directas, administradas por miembros de <a href="https://866ourvote.org/about/">la coalición no partidista Protección Electoral</a>, que pueden ayudarlo:</p>

<p>Inglés: 866-OUR-VOTE/866-687-8683, <a href="https://www.lawyerscommittee.org/project/election-protection/">The Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law</a></p>

<p>Español: 888-VE-Y-VOTA/888-839-8682, <a href="https://naleo.org/es/vota/">Fondo de Educación de la Asociación Nacional de Funcionarios Latinos Electos y Designados</a></p>

<p>Idiomas asiáticos: 888-API-VOTE/888-274-8683, <a href="https://apiavote.org/how-to-vote/multilingual-voter-hotline/">Voto Estadounidense de Asiáticos e Isleños del Pacífico</a></p>

<p>Árabe: 844-YALLA-US/844-925-5287, <a href="https://www.aaiusa.org/yalla-vote">Instituto Árabe Estadounidense</a></p>

<h2>Denuncie la intimidación de votantes</h2>

<p>Si alguien trata de asustarlo para que vote o para que no vote por un candidato, manténgase firme y exija una boleta en el sitio de votación, llame a una línea de ayuda  para denunciar la intimidación y más tarde presente una queja por teléfono ante el FBI al 800-CALL-FBI - 800-225-5324 - o por internet en <a href="https://tips.fbi.gov">tips.fbi.gov</a>.</p>

<h2>Demande</h2>

<p>Si aún no se le permite votar, considere emprender acciones legales, aunque primero obtenga asesoramiento sobre su situación particular en una de las líneas de ayuda, que cuentan con abogados gratuitos. Es buena idea anotar los nombres de las personas que le impidieron votar y pedir a las personas que presenciaron el incidente su información de contacto.</p>

<p><em>Esta es una versión actualizada de una noticia que se <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-to-do-if-your-vote-is-challenged-practical-advice-from-a-civil-rights-attorney-for-election-day-239066">publicó originalmente el 28 de octubre de 2024</a>.</em></p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291090/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Do you need to worry about the Sun turning into a black hole?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753184/original/file-20260810-50-8gb54v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C499%2C6004%2C4002&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption"> Black holes have a gravitational pull so strong that no objects close to them can escape. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/black-hole-illustration-royalty-free-illustration/2152055983?phrase=black+hole">Victor de Schwanberg/Science Photo Library via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure>

<blockquote>
<p><strong>Do I need to worry about the sun turning into a black hole? – Anonymous٫ age 7٫ Chicago٫ Illinois</strong></p>
</blockquote>

<hr>

<p>At the end of their lifespans, some massive stars collapse under their own weight until they <a href="https://theconversation.com/meet-lite-intermediate-black-holes-the-supermassive-black-holes-smaller-much-more-mysterious-cousin-259976">turn into a black hole</a> that sucks up everything around it. </p>

<p>It’s a dramatic conclusion to a star’s billions of years of existence, but it’s not the finale that our own Sun will have. Our solar system’s star is not big enough to have that kind of outcome, so worrying about the Sun becoming a black hole doesn’t need to be on your list of anxieties. Whatever happens to the Sun will happen very slowly, over billions of years. By that time, you’ll be long gone. Humans might not be there to witness it at all. </p>

<p>As an astrophysicist, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=5S7OeKEAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">I am</a> fascinated by <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cNOGE4_x3X0">black holes</a> and how they form. The universe is filled with different kinds of stars, and each has a distinct tale to tell about its life. </p>

<h2>Birth, life and death of a star</h2>

<p>Just like humans, stars have a life cycle. A star is born when a <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-first-stars-may-not-have-been-as-uniformly-massive-as-astronomers-thought-263016">giant gas cloud collapses in on itself</a> and <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/universe/stars/">then grows, shining light</a> by burning fuel. </p>

<p>In its core, the baby star fuses four atoms of hydrogen together to form the element helium, which releases energy in the form of starlight. This fuel-burning process also exerts outward pressure against gravity, which is pulling in on the star. These competing forces give stars their round shape.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753432/original/file-20260811-50-qwclua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A photo of the Sun, which is a bright sphere emitting light" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753432/original/file-20260811-50-qwclua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753432/original/file-20260811-50-qwclua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753432/original/file-20260811-50-qwclua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753432/original/file-20260811-50-qwclua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753432/original/file-20260811-50-qwclua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753432/original/file-20260811-50-qwclua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753432/original/file-20260811-50-qwclua.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The Sun burns bright by fusing together hydrogen atoms inside its core, which releases energy.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/gsfc/4923566097">NASA/GSFC/SOHO</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>As the star grows older, it eventually burns up all the hydrogen inside it. At this point, it can’t maintain the same outward push, so gravity squeezes the star, shrinking it smaller and smaller. The helium atoms inside are pushed closer together, and they start to <a href="https://theconversation.com/astrophysicists-use-space-archaeology-to-trace-the-history-of-a-spiral-galaxy-278948">fuse into heavier elements</a> such as carbon, oxygen, iron and more. </p>

<p>The star keeps burning its fuel and shining on until most of the helium in its core has fused into iron. But fusing together multiple atoms of iron requires taking in energy instead of releasing it, so at this point, the fuel burning stops. </p>

<p>Gravity then takes over, and the core of the star collapses rapidly in a dramatic explosion. The cores of heavier stars are extremely dense, so any material falling toward the collapsing star bounces off, producing shock waves. This phenomenon drives what is called a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JnFbG1cbLB0">core-collapse supernova explosion</a>. The star explodes, shooting elements like oxygen and other heavy elements off <a href="https://theconversation.com/elements-from-the-stars-the-unexpected-discovery-that-upended-astrophysics-66-years-ago-93916">into space</a>. What remains is a dead star with a small, dense core.  </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753186/original/file-20260810-50-mtbz2e.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A diagram showing the life cycle of the Sun, from its birth in a stellar nebula to its current state, then its growth into a red giant, red supergiant, planetary nebula and white dwarf" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753186/original/file-20260810-50-mtbz2e.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/753186/original/file-20260810-50-mtbz2e.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=300&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753186/original/file-20260810-50-mtbz2e.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=300&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753186/original/file-20260810-50-mtbz2e.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=300&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753186/original/file-20260810-50-mtbz2e.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=377&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753186/original/file-20260810-50-mtbz2e.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=377&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/753186/original/file-20260810-50-mtbz2e.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=377&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The life cycle of the Sun.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/sun-life-cycle-vector-royalty-free-illustration/1056774192?phrase=life%2Bcycle%2Bof%2Bthe%2Bsun">Mariia Domnikova/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Which stars will become black holes?</h2>

<p>The type of dead star the collapse forms depends on how much mass the star started with. If the mass is less than roughly eight times the mass of the Sun, the collapse will leave behind a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qsN1LglrX9s">white dwarf</a>. This is a star so dense that all <a href="https://www.energy.gov/science/doe-explainselectrons">the electrons</a> inside it are squeezed extremely close together, until they are no longer bound to individual atoms.</p>

<p>If the star was about eight to 20 times the mass of the Sun, it would leave behind a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=udFxKZRyQt4">neutron star</a>, which is an even denser star. In a neutron star, the electrons and protons crush together to produce neutrons. </p>

<p>If the star is heavier than 20 times the mass of the Sun, the end product will be a black hole with gravitational pull so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape past its boundary.</p>

<p>Because our Sun is on the smaller side for a star, when it dies it will collapse into a white dwarf, roughly the same size as Earth. It will still shine some light at first, but over time it may slowly cool down, to eventually become a cold, dark object called a <a href="https://www.space.com/23799-black-dwarfs.html">black dwarf</a>.</p>

<h2>Should you worry about the Sun’s future?</h2>

<p>In about 1 billion years from now, the Sun will start to grow hotter and brighter than it is today. As it shines more brightly, the sunlight it casts on Earth will increase, which will make the Earth hotter. The oceans will evaporate, and it will become very difficult to sustain life as we know it on Earth. </p>

<p>In about 5 billion years, all the hydrogen in the Sun’s core will run out. The core will then contract under gravity, while the hydrogen continues to fuse in a shell around it. This will cause the outer layer of the Sun to expand enormously and enter a phase known as the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/kYb404UeldQ">red giant</a>. During this phase, the Sun will grow so big that it could potentially run into Earth’s orbit. </p>

<p>Scientists don’t yet know if Earth will be swallowed by the Sun at this point. But even if Earth evades being gulped up, the Sun’s heat will toast everything on Earth, and no complex life will be able to survive.</p>

<p>This may sound scary, but you don’t have to worry, because humans will probably be long gone by the time the Sun starts <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-021-00693-5">consuming Earth’s atmosphere</a>.  </p>

<p>Earth was formed about <a href="https://www.nps.gov/subjects/geology/age-of-the-earth.htm">4.6 billion years ago</a>, and if you imagine its entire lifespan up to now as a single day, then all of human history happened in the last six seconds. There’s still about 26 hours to go before the Sun becomes a red giant.</p>

<h2>Is there any danger of being near a black hole?</h2>

<p>Suppose the Sun were to become a black hole today, all of sudden. Assuming the black hole had the same mass as the Sun, humans would not be in immediate danger. Earth and all other planets would feel the same gravitational pull as from the Sun.</p>

<p>Only objects very close to the black hole – within a few miles or so – would be sucked in. Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun, has an orbit of about 36 million miles (58 million kilometers).</p>

<p>This means there is no immediate danger from the Sun turning into a black hole, even hypothetically.</p>

Do I need to worry about the sun turning into a black hole? – Anonymous٫ age 7٫ Chicago٫ Illinois At the end of their lifespans, some massive stars collapse under their own weight until they turn into a black hole that sucks up everything around it
It’s a dramatic conclusion to a star’s billions of years of existence, but it’s not the finale that our own Sun will have
Our solar system’s star is not big enough to have that kind of outcome, so worrying about the Sun becoming a black hole doesn’t need to be on your list of anxieties
Whatever happens to the Sun will happen very slowly, over billions of years
Humans might not be there to witness it at all
As an astrophysicist, I am fascinated by black holes and how they form
The universe is filled with different kinds of stars, and each has a distinct tale to tell about its life
Birth, life and death of a star Just like humans, stars have a life cycle
A star is born when a giant gas cloud collapses in on itself and then grows, shining light by burning fuel
In its core, the baby star fuses four atoms of hydrogen together to form the element helium, which releases energy in the form of starlight
This fuel-burning process also exerts outward pressure against gravity, which is pulling in on the star
These competing forces give stars their round shape
The Sun burns bright by fusing together hydrogen atoms inside its core, which releases energy
NASA/GSFC/SOHO , CC BY As the star grows older, it eventually burns up all the hydrogen inside it
At this point, it can’t maintain the same outward push, so gravity squeezes the star, shrinking it smaller and smaller
The helium atoms inside are pushed closer together, and they start to fuse into heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen, iron and more
The star keeps burning its fuel and shining on until most of the helium in its core has fused into iron
But fusing together multiple atoms of iron requires taking in energy instead of releasing it, so at this point, the fuel burning stops
Gravity then takes over, and the core of the star collapses rapidly in a dramatic explosion
The cores of heavier stars are extremely dense, so any material falling toward the collapsing star bounces off, producing shock waves
This phenomenon drives what is called a core-collapse supernova explosion
The star explodes, shooting elements like oxygen and other heavy elements off into space
What remains is a dead star with a small, dense core
Mariia Domnikova/DigitalVision via Getty Images Which stars will become black holes? The type of dead star the collapse forms depends on how much mass the star started with
If the mass is less than roughly eight times the mass of the Sun, the collapse will leave behind a white dwarf
This is a star so dense that all the electrons inside it are squeezed extremely close together, until they are no longer bound to individual atoms
If the star was about eight to 20 times the mass of the Sun, it would leave behind a neutron star , which is an even denser star
In a neutron star, the electrons and protons crush together to produce neutrons
If the star is heavier than 20 times the mass of the Sun, the end product will be a black hole with gravitational pull so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape past its boundary
Because our Sun is on the smaller side for a star, when it dies it will collapse into a white dwarf, roughly the same size as Earth
It will still shine some light at first, but over time it may slowly cool down, to eventually become a cold, dark object called a black dwarf
Should you worry about the Sun’s future? In about 1 billion years from now, the Sun will start to grow hotter and brighter than it is today
As it shines more brightly, the sunlight it casts on Earth will increase, which will make the Earth hotter
The oceans will evaporate, and it will become very difficult to sustain life as we know it on Earth
In about 5 billion years, all the hydrogen in the Sun’s core will run out
The core will then contract under gravity, while the hydrogen continues to fuse in a shell around it
This will cause the outer layer of the Sun to expand enormously and enter a phase known as the red giant

<title>Stars and Stripes shows how government-funded journalism can work – if it’s free to report the truth</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757613/original/file-20260902-50-5m32rh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=267%2C0%2C4049%2C2699&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A drawing that appeared in an edition of Stars and Stripes depicts American troops participating in the predawn attack on Omaha Beach during D-Day on June 6, 1944.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/drawing-for-the-us-army-stars-and-stripes-newspaper-news-photo/489850649?adppopup=true">Ed Vebell/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As local and national news outlets <a href="https://localnewsinitiative.northwestern.edu/projects/state-of-local-news/2025/report/">continue to disappear across the U.S.</a>, I’d always thought that the military newspaper Stars and Stripes offered one model for a partial solution: government financial support.</p>

<p>But this approach only works if those who believe in the free press – including elected officials – offer unconditional support. </p>

<p>Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has not. </p>

<p>On Aug. 21, 2026, <a href="https://www.thewrap.com/media-platforms/journalism/pentagon-fires-stars-and-stripes-employees-insubordination/">the Pentagon fired the publisher, editor and a reporter</a> at Stars and Stripes, citing insubordination and unauthorized media appearances. But the firings took place after the outlet ran a string of articles that cast the Pentagon in a poor light.   </p>



<h2>A view from the front lines</h2>

<p>The newspaper, which is often simply called Stripes, has served overseas military forces and their families <a href="https://www.loc.gov/collections/stars-and-stripes/about-this-collection/">since 1918</a>, with a 23-year break between World War I and World War II.</p>

<p>It has continuously remained in print since World War II, providing Americans serving overseas on American military bases everywhere from Okinawa to the Azores with news on topics ranging from high school football games to troop deployments. </p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The editorial office for Stars and Stripes in Naples, Italy, pictured in 1944.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/front-line-newspaper-of-the-canadian-troops-in-italy-is-the-news-photo/499292077?adppopup=true">Toronto Star Archives/Toronto Star via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>When I was a reporter at Stars and Stripes in the late 1990s, I covered both the good and the bad from Bosnia and Kosovo during the NATO peacekeeping missions: the armed unit that doled out cash to Bosnians after the military ran over their farm animals; the soldiers who guarded a school so that the children of separate ethnic groups could attend together; and the military contractors who received no-bid contracts.</p>

<p>While some big stories are also written about in other news outlets covering the military, many of them are only discovered because Stars and Stripes’ civilian and military journalists work and live alongside service members in Europe, the Middle East and the Pacific. </p>

<p>It’s the very same premise behind good local newspapers: There’s little meaningful journalism about local issues without journalists who live and work in the communities they cover. </p>

<p>Stripes was able to provide <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/The-Stars-and-stripes-:-World-War-II-and-the-early-years/oclc/18052597">the only eyewitness account</a> of the negotiations that led to Germany’s surrender in 1945 because its reporter was in the schoolhouse in Reims, France, where Allied and German officials hashed out the terms. </p>

<p>Stripes journalists were also on the front lines of the Vietnam War, with The New York Times describing Stars and Stripes as the only military information outlet <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1970/04/12/archives/how-the-gis-in-vietnam-dont-learn-about-the-war-gis-news-and-the.html">giving American troops in Vietnam a candid account of the war’s progress</a>. </p>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/members-of-battery-a-7th-battalion-8th-artillery-read-the-news-photo/599753443?adppopup=true">PhotoQuest/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>More recently, a Stripes reporter based in Bahrain was able to report how U.S. military families were experiencing <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/investigations/2026/02/28/where-us-attack-iran-images-video/">Iranian drone attacks in Manama</a>, which hosts the headquarters of the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet. She was able to report on the attacks firsthand <a href="https://www.stripes.com/theaters/middle_east/2026-05-28/bahrain-return-21805839.html">because she was right there</a>, evacuating alongside them.</p>

<h2>Reporters clash with the Pentagon</h2>

<p>It was another Stars and Stripes journalist who first reported on <a href="https://www.stripes.com/theaters/middle_east/2026-07-09/abraham-lincoln-middle-east-sailor-mental-health-22219830.html">the problems aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln</a> in July and August 2026.</p>

<p>The aircraft carrier was in the midst of an exceedingly long deployment due to the U.S.-Iran war. There had been food and water shortages, disrupted mail service and long, grueling workdays with little time off. Some sailors were experiencing <a href="https://www.stripes.com/theaters/middle_east/2026-07-09/abraham-lincoln-middle-east-sailor-mental-health-22219830.html">mental health struggles</a>, and at least one jumped overboard. </p>

<p>The reporter, Alison Bath, who is based at the headquarters of the U.S. Navy’s Sixth Fleet in Naples, Italy, had interviewed active-duty sailors and family members of sailors aboard the ship. She explained how she had reviewed “<a href="https://www.stripes.com/theaters/us/2026-08-11/abraham-lincoln-middle-east-mental-health-town-hall-meeting-22506344.html">dozens of public social media comments and posts</a> by crew members.” </p>

<p>Bath’s story and the follow-up accounts from other media outlets clearly angered Hegseth, who said it “<a href="https://www.stripes.com/branches/navy/2026-08-15/lincoln-cao-trump-hegseth-mental-health-22560145.html">completely misrepresented</a>” the situation.</p>

<p>The media frenzy over the USS Lincoln largely overshadowed the work of another Stripes journalist, Lara Korte, who reported on the <a href="https://www.stripes.com/branches/navy/2026-08-21/bahrain-evacuation-military-families-navy-22618186.html">hardships, confusion and financial costs</a> endured by military families who had to suddenly evacuate from U.S. Central Command headquarters in Bahrain starting on March 2, 2026. </p>

<p>Like Bath, Korte had interviewed several military family members, one of whom shared with Korte the audio recording of a virtual town hall meeting that the military held for the families. A Navy admiral said on the recording that the military “was in uncharted territory” and had little guidance for families who didn’t know where to live or how to retrieve their cars and belongings.</p>

<p>Though the Pentagon didn’t dispute Korte’s reporting, she was fired for “insubordination” alongside the editor-in-chief, Erik Slavin, and publisher, Max Lederer, on Aug. 21.</p>

<p>Bath is still employed by the paper.</p>

<h2>You can’t manufacture credibility</h2>

<p>Unlike most shuttered or shrunken news outlets <a href="https://www.theatlantic.com/business/archive/2016/11/the-print-apocalypse-and-how-to-survive-it/506429/">whose advertising model was upended by the internet</a>, Stars and Stripes has long been shielded from market forces thanks to a subsidy from the Department of Defense <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/22/nx-s1-5941159/after-high-profile-firings-by-the-pentagon-is-stars-stripes-still-independent">that covers roughly half its budget</a>.</p>

<p>While this funding could be seen as anathema to journalistic independence, the U.S. government has <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0196859910388278">mandated since the 1950s</a> that the paper have editorial freedom. </p>

<p>Even before then, U.S. military leaders protected the newspaper’s independence. <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/10021785">Gen. John J. Pershing</a>, who commanded the American Expeditionary Forces in Europe during World War I, and Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower, who commanded Allied forces in Europe during World War II, each <a href="https://encyclopedia.1914-1918-online.net/bibliography/u24iij55/">ordered military commanders</a> <a href="https://www.gao.gov/products/nsiad-89-60">not to interfere with the newspaper</a>. So did <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1970/04/12/archives/how-the-gis-in-vietnam-dont-learn-about-the-war-gis-news-and-the.html">Navy Adm. John S. McCain Jr.</a>, father of the late Sen. John McCain and the commander‐in‐chief of U.S. Pacific Command during the Vietnam War.</p>

<p>That’s not what’s happening under the Trump administration.</p>

<p>In <a href="https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/27880913/modernization-of-stars-and-stripes-operations-osd002139-26-res-final.pdf">March 2026</a>, the Pentagon instituted new guidelines requiring that Stripes content be “consistent with good order and discipline of the military.” The following month, <a href="http://stripes.com/opinion/2026-04-23/stripes-former-ombudsman-pentagon-trying-to-silence-21465037.html?">the department fired Jacqueline Smith</a>, the newspaper’s ombudsman charged with protecting its editorial independence.</p>

<p>Chief Pentagon spokesperson <a href="https://thehill.com/people/sean-parnell/">Sean Parnell</a> described the moves as part of an effort to “refocus” the outlet away from “<a href="https://www.poynter.org/commentary/2026/stars-and-stripes-pentagon-military-journalism/">woke distractions that siphon morale</a>.”</p>



<p>There’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/13688804.2010.483092">always been a struggle</a> between military leaders who want to control the reporting at Stripes and those who recognize that freedom of the press is exactly the kind of right that the U.S. military fights for. </p>

<p>Many current and former military commanders see a real benefit in the outlet’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0196859910388278">editorial independence</a> because of the values it communicates and the information it provides</p>

<p>Retired Army Lt. Gen. Mark Hertling is one such supporter. In an Aug. 25, 2026, article in The Bulwark website, <a href="https://www.thebulwark.com/p/the-pentagons-purge-at-stars-and-stripes-hegseth-firing-military-newspaper-aircraft-carrier-iran-war?">he described the ways in which</a> he relied on the newspaper’s reporting when he was a commander in Europe. </p>

<p>“Every major military command has an extensive communications apparatus,” Hertling wrote, “but none of those organizations can manufacture credibility. Credibility comes from readers believing that when something goes wrong, somebody will tell them. That’s why Stripes’ early reporting on the USS Abraham Lincoln was so important.”</p>

<h2>Public media only works with no strings attached</h2>

<p>On Aug. 27, the fired publisher, editor and reporter <a href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.295983/gov.uscourts.dcd.295983.1.0.pdf">filed a lawsuit</a> against Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell, the Defense Department, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and another public affairs official, Andrew Brey, alleging <a href="https://www.stripes.com/theaters/us/2026-08-27/fired-stripes-employees-lawsuit-pentagon-22676947.html">that they were fired in retaliation</a> for news coverage that was unflattering to the military. The suit argues that this violated both their protected rights to free speech and Department of Defense policies and regulations.</p>

<p>The department hasn’t specifically responded to the allegations, <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/28/stars-and-stripes-journalists-facing-firing-get-one-week-reprieve-01055447">but it did agree to a one-week reprieve of paid administrative leave</a> as a federal judge considers the lawsuit.</p>

<p>The three journalists are being represented by the same legal team that represents the fired former employees of Voice of America, another government-funded news source that the Trump administration <a href="https://www.npr.org/2025/04/22/nx-s1-5372530/voa-trump-radio-free-asia">attempted to dismantle in 2025</a>. Like Stripes, Voice of America received government funding even as it sometimes reported unfavorably on the government. <a href="https://jmoreliving.com/2019/04/17/honoring-the-courage-and-sacrifice-of-paul-savanuck/">And like journalists at Stripes</a>, Voice of America reporters <a href="https://www.voanews.com/a/gunmen-kill-voa-reporter-in-pakistan-137485033/150771.html">have died doing their jobs</a>.</p>

<p>But despite the Trump White House’s <a href="https://www.poynter.org/business-work/2026/trump-press-freedom/">unrelenting attacks on public, nonprofit and for-profit media outlets</a>, the government funding model <a href="https://niemanreports.org/state-public-funding-local-news/">is having some success</a> at the state level. The organization Rebuild Local News estimates that states <a href="https://www.poynter.org/business-work/2026/state-government-support-local-news-journalism/">will spend US$74 million supporting local journalism</a> in 2026 via fellowships, media training, tax credits and more.</p>

<p>While the group’s leaders say these initiatives demand constant scrutiny to ensure there’s no creeping government interference or political strings attached to the funds, <a href="https://knightcolumbia.org/blog/reimagining-and-reconstructing-us-public-media">many supporters of local journalism see promise in this model</a>. Government funding for independent media has long existed in Europe, Australia, New Zealand and elsewhere. Some of these outlets <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2018/06/08/western-europe-public-news-media-widely-used-and-trusted/">are widely trusted by the public</a>.</p>

<p>But that trust doesn’t come easily. It requires political and military leaders to repeatedly reaffirm the ideal of a free and independent press – even when the coverage doesn’t go their way.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290477/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Compared to driving, flying is extraordinarily safe – but why doesn’t it feel that way?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754379/original/file-20260817-49-i1bz2r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2256%2C1504&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Millions of people fly safely every day, but when plane crashes do happen, they can be catastrophic. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.flickr.com/photos/themarinegeek/12305099684/">RM Bulseco/Flickr</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A commercial airplane crash can change how people behave long after the immediate tragedy. News outlets replay the images, people affected share their harrowing stories, and an extraordinarily rare event becomes easy to imagine. Some travelers cancel trips; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0956-7976.2004.00668.x">others drive to their destination instead</a>. </p>

<p>These choices may feel cautious. Statistically, the alternatives people switch to may come with greater risk.</p>

<p>Commercial airline crashes command attention because they are rare, catastrophic and beyond a passenger’s control. But the choice to avoid flying does not eliminate risk. <a href="https://commons.erau.edu/bcaas-reports/1/">As a new report from our research team at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University outlines</a>, skipping a flight and opting to drive instead is typically much riskier, even if it doesn’t feel like it.</p>

<h2>Airline travel is safer than headlines suggest</h2>

<p>People tend to respond strongly to events that are vivid, while paying less attention to familiar hazards – the risks of which manifest more frequently but less visibly. As a result, efforts to avoid one danger can create another.</p>

<p>In <a href="https://commons.erau.edu/bcaas-reports/1/">our recent peer-reviewed report</a>, prepared with support from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University’s Boeing Center for Aviation and Aerospace Safety, we compared fatality risk in U.S. commercial aviation with other transportation modes, recreational activities, household hazards and occupational risks. While the Boeing Center receives some funding from The Boeing Company, it operates independently.</p>

<p>We focused on <a href="https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/air_carriers/operations/part_121">commercial Part 121 airlines</a> operating in the U.S. and analyzed data from 2016 through 2025. Part 121 carriers generally include large U.S. airlines and regional carriers that operate scheduled passenger service. Because fatal accidents are so rare, data from a single year would not have provided a stable risk estimate. </p>

<p>Across several measures of risk exposure, including distance traveled, individual boardings, hours spent traveling, annual risk and lifetime odds, the data <a href="https://commons.erau.edu/bcaas-reports/1/">consistently shows</a> that U.S. commercial aviation is exceptionally safe.</p>

<p>For the same distance traveled, we estimated the fatality risk as <a href="https://commons.erau.edu/bcaas-reports/1/">about 626 times higher in a passenger car or truck</a> than on a commercial airline. The risk associated with motorcycle travel was more than 22,000 times higher than commercial airline travel. Even highway bus travel, itself a relatively safe option, carried about nine times the risk of commercial airline travel over the same distance.</p>

<p>When risk is measured per passenger boarding, the numbers remain striking. From 2016 through 2024, the long-run estimate was approximately <a href="https://commons.erau.edu/bcaas-reports/1/">one passenger fatality per 97.7 million boardings</a> on commercial airlines. </p>

<p>These numbers do not mean flying is risk-free, just that the risk is small enough that researchers need many years and enormous amounts of exposure to estimate it. Across the 10-year study period, 73 people died in accidents involving commercial airline travel in the United States.</p>

<p>These findings complement earlier research. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.retrec.2012.12.011">A peer-reviewed 2013 study comparing U.S. transportation modes</a> examined data from 2000 through 2009 and also identified commercial aviation as the safest way to travel. A <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/risa.12693">2018 study</a> using data from the same period similarly ranked commercial aviation as the safest mode.</p>

<p>More recently, a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/sf/soab114">2022 study</a> analyzed U.S. news coverage, travel patterns and accident data from 1996 through 2017. It found that increased news coverage of aviation accidents was associated with more road traffic and more fatal road accidents in subsequent months. </p>

<h2>The 9/11 aftermath and the risk of avoiding risk</h2>

<p>The aftermath of the <a href="https://www.history.com/articles/9-11-attacks">Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks</a> provided a powerful example of how behavior can shift risk from one setting to another. <a href="https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/6329">Air travel declined sharply</a> after the 9/11 attacks. Subsequently, researchers were able to investigate whether fear of flying led to additional deaths on the road.</p>

<p>Psychologist <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0956-7976.2004.00668.x">Gerd Gigerenzer analyzed traffic patterns</a> for the final three months of 2001 and estimated 353 excess road deaths nationwide. He characterized many people’s decision to drive rather than fly as an attempt to avoid a “dread risk”: a low-probability event in which many people could die at once.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754947/original/file-20260819-50-2zhw2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Four lanes of traffic on a highway" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754947/original/file-20260819-50-2zhw2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754947/original/file-20260819-50-2zhw2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=380&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754947/original/file-20260819-50-2zhw2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=380&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754947/original/file-20260819-50-2zhw2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=380&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754947/original/file-20260819-50-2zhw2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=478&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754947/original/file-20260819-50-2zhw2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=478&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754947/original/file-20260819-50-2zhw2o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=478&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">After a high-profile plane crash, road traffic can increase.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=traffic&amp;mediaType=photo&amp;vs=true">AP Photo/LM Otero, File</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Transportation researchers <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trf.2004.09.007">Michael Sivak and Michael Flannagan later reanalyzed the period</a>. They used road fatality trends from the first eight months of 2000 and 2001 to estimate how many deaths would normally have occurred during the final three months of 2001. They then compared that estimate with the number actually recorded in the past three months and calculated 1,018 additional road fatalities from October 2001 through December 2001.</p>

<p>But their findings complicated the idea that people who avoided flying merely drove to the same distant destinations. <a href="https://news.umich.edu/roadway-deaths-up-after-9-11-due-largely-to-local-driving/">Much of the increase occurred on local roads</a>, not interstate highways, and pedestrians and bicyclists experienced a disproportionate share of fatalities. This pattern suggests that travel behavior may have changed more broadly after the attacks, perhaps because people canceled longer trips, stayed closer to home or changed their daily routines.</p>

<p>It is hard to pin down how much of this increase was related to people changing their travel patterns in response to the 9/11 attacks, since these studies cannot track each individual’s transportation decisions. </p>

<p>But both studies suggest that a collective effort to avoid a highly visible danger can increase exposure to ordinary hazards whose victims are less visible. When more people choose to drive rather than fly, the roads become busier and the number of traffic deaths can rise.</p>

<h2>The question shapes the risk estimate</h2>

<p>One reason discussions about risk become confusing is that there is no single way to measure it. The answer to the question “Is it safe?” depends on what you measure.</p>

<p>How much risk does a person face for each mile traveled? What is the risk of one trip? How much risk accumulates during one hour of travel? What is the chance of dying from this cause in a year or over a lifetime?</p>

<p>These are legitimate questions, but to make a valid comparison, you need to look at the same measure of risk for both types of transportation. Comparing the risk of one flight with the annual risk of driving, for example, mixes unlike quantities. </p>

<p>A traveler deciding whether to fly or drive between two cities can compare the two modes over the same trip or distance. This comparison provides a clearer perspective than comparing a highly visible plane crash with a familiar daily routine.</p>

<p>Time matters too. In our estimates, an hour in a passenger car or truck carried about <a href="https://commons.erau.edu/bcaas-reports/1/">74 times the fatality risk</a> of an hour aboard a commercial aircraft. </p>

<h2>Feeling in control is not the same as safety</h2>

<p>Driving gives people a steering wheel, a brake pedal and the belief that their skill can protect them. Flying asks passengers to place control in the hands of pilots, airlines, regulators, air traffic controllers and a complex technical system. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actpsy.2019.04.015">Psychological research has linked</a> a stronger sense of agency – the feeling that people control their actions and their outcomes – with greater risk-taking. That difference in perceived control helps explain why a rare aviation disaster can feel more threatening than routine road travel.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754948/original/file-20260819-50-ufg92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A shadowed traveler pulling a suitcase through an airport, with the tail of an airplane visible out the window." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754948/original/file-20260819-50-ufg92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754948/original/file-20260819-50-ufg92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=371&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754948/original/file-20260819-50-ufg92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=371&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754948/original/file-20260819-50-ufg92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=371&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754948/original/file-20260819-50-ufg92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=466&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754948/original/file-20260819-50-ufg92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=466&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754948/original/file-20260819-50-ufg92v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=466&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Airline passengers don’t have the same sense of control over their vehicle as drivers, so flying can feel more uncertain and dangerous.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=air%20travel&amp;mediaType=photo&amp;vs=true">AP Photo/Susan Walsh</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Media attention also matters. A major airplane crash is treated as news of national or international importance. <a href="https://www.iihs.org/research-areas/fatality-statistics/detail/state-by-state">Road deaths occur</a> across many locations and at different times, so the public does not see the cumulative toll. </p>

<p>The emotional intensity of coverage does not mean journalists are wrong to cover crashes. It just means audiences need context alongside the images.</p>

<h2>Crafting better risk communication</h2>

<p>Telling anxious travelers that flying is “safe” is rarely enough. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028279">Research on risk perception</a> shows that people do not judge danger through statistics alone. Fear and vivid images also shape how risky an event feels. But providing more context about the risks from other forms of transportation can still help.</p>

<p>Effective communication about risk does not minimize tragedy or dismiss the real fear people may feel. But it can help people understand that when millions of travelers shift from one type of transportation to another, the risk moves with them.</p>

<p>For travelers, the practical question is not whether an option has zero risk. No option does. The question is whether a choice reduces their total exposure to risk or merely replaces a frightening, highly visible risk with a greater one that feels routine.</p>

<p>To put the rarity of fatal airline events into perspective, an average of <a href="https://www.tsa.gov/news/press/releases/2025/11/21/golden-age-travel-tsa-prepared-screen-more-3-million-thanksgiving">2.48 million travelers</a> passed through TSA screening each day in 2025. Modern commercial aviation in the United States has achieved a safety record that is difficult to grasp precisely because fatal events are so unusual. </p>

<p>When fear leads people away from that system, the safest-feeling decision may not be the safest decision at all.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289559/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: The face of American feminism

body: American feminist leader and author Gloria Steinem photographed in San Francisco in 1977. | Janet Fries/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day
Gloria Steinem — the one-woman powerhouse who, in many ways, defined modern feminism in the United States — died Wednesday at 92 after six decades of activism
Steinem was a journalist and advocate who first rose to prominence in the late 1960s, just as the women’s liberation movement exploded

She co-founded Ms. magazine, a trailblazing publication that mainstreamed once-taboo topics like sexual harassment, wage inequity, and the unfair division of household labor.  As an advocate, Steinem also led protests, worked to elect more female politicians, and lobbied for abortion rights, employment protections, and the long-deferred Equal Rights Amendment
The ERA, which would create a constitutional guarantee of equal rights for women, has never officially been adopted , despite being ratified by the required number of states

Many of the other causes Steinem championed, however, are now at least firmly part of mainstream cultural and political debate.   Later in life, as the feminist movement evolved, Steinem continued to serve as a kind of elder statesperson. (We’ll break down how exactly it evolved in just a minute.) Much of her recent writing and speaking focused — for obvious, depressing reasons — on the importance of hope and persistence in social justice movements. “Hope is a form of planning,” she told Vogue on her 90th birthday, in 2024. “If you don’t imagine what could be, you’re already defeated.” Heads up: Vox is off tomorrow and Monday for the Labor Day holiday

And speaking of labor…can I interest you in supporting all the work that goes into this newsletter? For a limited time, you can become a Vox member — and invest in the journalism that helps you think more deeply about the world — for just $30/year
Go a little deeper Steinem was the single-most recognizable face of American feminism, but she represented a distinct wave of it that future generations of feminists built on

American feminism is a sprawling, evolving, multifaceted movement — and its history is often broken down into four distinct periods .  First wave: 1848 to 1920 : You might better know the feminists of this era by the name “suffragists”: The troublesome campaigners who fought for women’s right to vote
This “wave,” as it’s popularly dubbed, began with the Seneca Falls convention in New York and ended with the passage of the 19th Amendment, after which momentum died down a bit
Second wave: 1963 to the 1980s : The movement revived with the publication of Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique in 1963
It also broadened its focus beyond political rights, taking on reproductive freedom, workplace and cultural sexism, sexual harassment, and women’s financial independence
Steinem was maybe the quintessential second-wave feminist
Third wave: 1991 to the 2000s : Feminism slumped a bit in the ’80s, deflated by Reagan-era conservatism and a backlash that cast feminists as bitter, bra-burning man-haters
But the Anita Hill case in 1991 revived mainstream attention to workplace harassment, discrimination and women’s exclusion from positions of power
Fourth wave: 2008(ish) to present : The current generation of feminism places greater emphasis on intersectionality and trans inclusion
But its defining trait is probably how very online it is
The fourth wave kicked off with blogs like Jezebel and Feministing and picked up steam through hashtags like #MeToo, #TimesUp, #StandWithWendy, and #YesAllWomen
In fairness, not everyone is terribly enamored with the “waves” framework
But for those of us trying to get the gist of recent history — or to take stock of what has and hasn’t changed, on the occasion of Steinem’s death — it can be a helpful way to get oriented
Vox has lots of further reading if you want to get into the nuances
One link for later ➨ Talk to your aging parents about their Apple Watches
Wearable devices like the Apple Watch can serve as alert systems that help keep older people safe

But before you buy a fitness tracker or a smart camera to keep an eye on your loved one , have a serious chat with them about their wishes and privacy.  Before you go… Did you know… that the iconic orange carrot we eat today wasn’t popularized until the 1600s , when they were bred by Dutch farmers? Prior to that, only the white, yellow, and purple varieties were commonly available

Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you which iconic web portal uses the butterfly logo
That would be MSN, originally “Microsoft Network,” which first debuted 31 years ago.
